summary: Researched WCAG 2.2 (W3C), Nielsen Norman Group, GOV.UK Design System / GOV.UK content guidance, Home Office design, and peer-reviewed low-literacy HCI reviews, then audited the existing Lumiere frontend (D:\FYP\frontend\src) against them. The headline conclusion: inclusive design for low-literacy, low-skill, elderly and non-English-first users is NOT a separate "accessible mode" — every change below also measurably helps expert users (NN/g's low-literacy rewrite lifted task success 46%→82% and cut task time from 22.3 to 9.5 minutes, with higher-literacy users gaining on all three metrics too). Three cross-cutting rules emerge: (1) never make meaning depend on one channel alone — not on colour, not on an icon, not on a hover, not on a transient toast; (2) make the default path the simple path and put power behind one clearly-labelled door, never two; (3) make every destructive act reversible so the UI never has to ask "are you sure?". The audit found concrete, fixable violations already baked into the shared primitives: every single button size in src/components/ui/button.tsx (h-6/h-7/h-8/h-9 = 24/28/32/36px) is below the 44px WCAG 2.5.5 AAA target and below Apple's 44pt and Material's 48dp floors; mobile nav labels are text-[10px]; "coming soon" nav states use /35 and /40 opacity (contrast failure) and explain themselves only via a title tooltip that touch users can never see; the dashboard's empty states are literal em-dashes ("—"); login errors fire into an auto-dismissing sonner toast with no inline message, no error summary and no aria-describedby; and the dashboard's flagship card explains "JWT token", "Django API" and "CORS" to a wardrobe user. Fixing these in the primitives (button.tsx, badge.tsx, globals.css, plus a new EmptyState and FieldError component) propagates the fix to every screen you build in phases 2-6, which is far cheaper than retrofitting 8 feature areas later.

findings.title: Target the reading level explicitly: 6th grade on entry pages, 8th grade elsewhere, sentences under 25 words
findings.detail: NN/g recommends text at a 6th-grade reading level on the homepage, important category pages and landing pages, and an 8th-grade level on other pages, noting about half of US adults read at 8th grade or below while most sites are written at 10th grade or higher. GOV.UK's clear-language guidance is harder-edged and gives you testable limits: split any sentence over 25 words, no paragraph longer than 5 sentences, active voice not passive, use contractions like 'you'll' but avoid negative contractions like 'can't'/'don't' (low-literacy and non-native readers misread the negation), and replace formal words with short ones ('buy' not 'purchase', 'help' not 'assist', 'about' not 'approximately'). GOV.UK notes 1 in 6 adults in England have very poor literacy skills. Words ending in -ion and -ment are a reliable smell for an over-complex sentence. WCAG 3.1.5 Reading Level (AAA) sets the formal bar at 'lower secondary education level' (roughly 7-9 years of schooling) or else a simpler version must be available. Home Office guidance for people with limited English recommends an average sentence length of 15 words. Plain-language practice targets Flesch Reading Ease 65+ / Flesch-Kincaid grade 6-9 and >50% active voice.
findings.actionable: Create D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\copy.ts as the single home for all user-facing strings (it also becomes your i18n message catalogue later) and enforce three rules in review: max 25 words per sentence, max 15-word average, max 5 sentences per paragraph. Add a CI check that runs a readability scorer over that file and fails the build above grade 8. Immediately rewrite the login page subtitle and dashboard greeting: 'Add your city in settings so we can pull your local weather' → 'Tell us your city. Then we can show you the weather.' (two short sentences, active, no 'pull' as jargon).

findings.title: Lower-literacy users PLOW text line-by-line instead of scanning, so layout must be single-column and front-loaded
findings.detail: This is the single most design-relevant finding in the NN/g low-literacy research: lower-literacy users do not scan. They read word-for-word, line by line, with a narrow field of view, and they cannot glance at a block and extract the gist. Consequences NN/g draws directly: use one main content column rather than multi-column layouts (a two-dimensional layout forces scanning they cannot do); put the main point at the very top of the page because these readers give up after a few lines; keep important information above the fold because scrolling breaks their visual concentration and they lose their place; avoid dense text blocks, which get skipped entirely; prefer static text over animation and fly-out menus that move or change; and use linear navigation menus in a straightforward sequence rather than menus that must be hunted. Search must tolerate misspellings and give short easy summaries, ideally answering the query in the first result.
findings.actionable: Keep the dashboard's existing mx-auto max-w-6xl but drop the lg:grid-cols-3 / sm:grid-cols-2 card grids on any screen whose content is instructional — a 4-across stat grid is exactly the 2D scan pattern that fails. For the phase-2 closet screens: one column of content on mobile, and never put the primary action below the fold. When you build wardrobe search, make the backend query trigram/fuzzy (Postgres pg_trgm) so 'jakit' finds 'jacket' — misspelling tolerance is an accessibility feature here, not a nice-to-have. Replace the hover-dependent sidebar title="Coming in a later phase" with visible static text.

findings.title: Never ship an icon-only control: only home, print and magnifying-glass are universally understood, and labels must be always visible
findings.detail: NN/g's icon research is unusually blunt: across decades of testing only three icons approach true universal recognition — home, print, and the magnifying glass for search. Everything else is ambiguous because usage is inconsistent across products (heart vs star for save/favourite/rate is the classic collision; in one study a non-standard clock icon for navigation history was clicked by not a single test participant). The governing rule is 'Icon labels should be visible at all times, without any interaction from the user' — hover-revealed labels fail because they raise interaction cost and simply do not exist on touch devices, which is how most of your low-skill users will arrive. NN/g's 5-second rule is a useful design gate: if you need more than 5 seconds to think of an appropriate icon for a concept, an icon cannot communicate that concept. A text label is also what makes the control translatable, which matters for non-English-first users.
findings.actionable: Delete the icon, icon-xs, icon-sm and icon-lg size variants from D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\button.tsx, or rename them to icon-only-requires-justification so they cannot be reached casually. Your wardrobe domain has zero universal icons: the Shirt, Scan (Fitting Room), Sparkles (Steal the Look), WashingMachine (In the wash) and MapPin (Storage) glyphs in nav-items.ts and dashboard/page.tsx are all ambiguous and must keep their text label everywhere they appear, including in the topbar and in any item-card overflow menu. For the item card actions you will build in phase 2 (wear, wash, delete, move), use labelled buttons or a labelled 'More actions' menu — never a bare ellipsis-and-trash row. Where an icon-only control is genuinely unavoidable, add both aria-label and a visible adjacent label.

findings.title: Every button size in button.tsx fails the 44px touch floor — rebuild the size scale around 44/48px
findings.detail: The numbers converge from four independent directions. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, requires at least 24x24 CSS pixels, with a spacing exception measured precisely: an imaginary 24 CSS pixel diameter circle centred on each target's bounding box must not intersect another target's circle. WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA, raises that to 44x44 CSS pixels. Apple HIG requires a minimum tappable area of 44x44 pt; Material Design requires 48x48 dp. The physiological basis is the MIT Touch Lab finding that the average finger pad is 10-14mm and fingertip 8-10mm. Guidance for older adults explicitly recommends going past both platform minimums to 48x48 because arthritis and tremor make precise tapping unreliable, and specifically flags dropdowns and sliders as high-failure controls for declining motor skills. Your current scale is default h-8 (32px), xs h-6 (24px), sm h-7 (28px), lg h-9 (36px), icon size-8 (32px), icon-xs size-6 (24px), icon-sm size-7 (28px), icon-lg size-9 (36px). Not one reaches 44px; xs and icon-xs sit exactly on the AA floor with zero margin, so any adjacent control breaks even AA via the spacing rule.
findings.actionable: Rewrite the size variants in D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\button.tsx: make default h-11 (44px), lg h-12 (48px) as the primary-action size, sm h-11 with tighter px (shrink padding, never height), and delete xs entirely. Set every icon variant to size-11 minimum. Apply the same to input.tsx, select.tsx and checkbox.tsx — a 16px shadcn checkbox needs either a h-11 wrapping label as the hit area or explicit min-h-11. Add a Tailwind utility in globals.css, e.g. @utility tap-target { min-height: 44px; min-width: 44px; }, and make it the reviewable token you grep for. Enforce at least 8px (gap-2) between any two adjacent tap targets so the 24px-circle spacing rule can never be violated. For the phase-3 calendar and any rating/slider control, provide a tap-based alternative rather than a drag or a thin slider.

findings.title: 16px is the absolute minimum body text — your mobile nav labels are 10px and text-xs is used for real content
findings.detail: Guidance for older audiences sets 16px as the absolute floor for body text, with some research recommending larger, and requires that the app respect the user's system-level font size. Ageing eyes lose sharpness, struggle to distinguish colours, and gain glare sensitivity; the low-contrast greys fashionable in modern UI are singled out as a usability disaster for aging eyes. Shades of blue in particular appear faded to seniors. Your codebase currently ships text-[10px] labels in mobile-nav.tsx, text-[10px] 'soon' badges and text-[11px] footer text in sidebar.tsx, text-[11px] phase chips and text-xs (12px) stat-card labels in dashboard/page.tsx, and text-sm (14px) as the default button label and the default body size. The mobile nav labels are the worst case because for a low-literacy user that label IS the control (per the icon finding above) — a 10px label is functionally an icon-only button.
findings.actionable: In D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\globals.css set the base body size to 1rem/16px explicitly and define a type scale whose smallest step is 0.875rem/14px, reserved for genuinely secondary metadata only — never for a label, a control, an error, or an instruction. Change mobile-nav.tsx text-[10px] to text-xs at minimum and preferably text-sm with shorter labels ('Closet' not 'My Closet', 'Calendar', 'Try on', 'Shop'). Raise the button.tsx default text from text-sm to text-base. Delete the text-[10px] and text-[11px] literals in sidebar.tsx and dashboard/page.tsx. Never set a fixed px font-size on html, so browser/OS zoom keeps working.

findings.title: Stop dimming with opacity — /35, /40 and /50 opacity states are contrast failures, and disabled controls should be avoided entirely
findings.detail: GOV.UK's button guidance says plainly to avoid disabled buttons because 'disabled buttons have poor contrast and can confuse some users'. Opacity-based dimming is the same problem expressed in CSS: it multiplies against the background and silently drops text below the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 threshold. Your code has four instances: sidebar.tsx renders unbuilt pages at text-sidebar-foreground/35 with a badge at text-sidebar-accent-foreground/60, mobile-nav.tsx at text-muted-foreground/40, the sidebar footer at /40, and button.tsx applies a global disabled:opacity-50. Worse, the only explanation of WHY those nav items are inert is a title="Coming in a later phase" tooltip — NN/g's error-reporting guidance explicitly says not to use tooltips for important information because they require hover/focus and are invisible on touch. For a low-skill user, a greyed unexplained row reads as 'the app is broken'.
findings.actionable: In D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\layout\sidebar.tsx and mobile-nav.tsx, replace the /35 and /40 opacity with a full-contrast foreground colour plus a visible text badge reading 'Not ready yet' (sentence case, no uppercase tracking, no 10px). Better still per GOV.UK: don't render an inert control at all — either omit unbuilt pages from the nav, or let them link to a real page that says what the feature will do and what to do meanwhile. Replace button.tsx's disabled:opacity-50 with a distinct, still-readable style, and for the login/register submit buttons keep the button enabled and validate on submit rather than disabling it. Audit globals.css's --muted-foreground (oklch 0.53) wherever it lands on --muted, and drop --warning (oklch 0.75 0.15 75, roughly 2:1 on white) from any text or icon role — use it for fills only with a darker paired foreground.

findings.title: Empty states must do three jobs: say why it's empty, teach what goes here, and give a button that starts the task
findings.detail: NN/g's three guidelines for empty states in complex applications are: (1) Communicate system status — never leave a panel blank, and never show a wrong status like 'No records' while data is still loading, because misleading messages make users 'develop a severe distrust of and distaste for the application'; (2) Provide learning cues — explain what could populate the area and how the feature works, citing DataDog's 'Star your favorites to list them here' as the model; (3) Provide direct pathways for key tasks — an actual button or step-by-step instructions, not a vague descriptive suggestion, with Loggly's two-path empty state (add a real source, or explore with demo data) as the exemplar. NN/g frames the empty state as the 'teachable moment' and notes that in-context learning cues shown as the user starts a task are generally more successful than forced tutorials at first use, because in-context help can be applied immediately and is therefore more memorable. This is the single highest-leverage pattern for your audience: the first screen a new user sees is, by definition, empty.
findings.actionable: Build D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\empty-state.tsx taking {illustration, heading, whatGoesHere, primaryAction, secondaryAction} and use it in every phase-2..6 list (closet, storage, calendar, outfits, marketplace, swaps). Replace the four dashboard stat cards whose value is the em-dash "—" in D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\(app)\dashboard\page.tsx: 'Items owned —' becomes 'No clothes added yet' + a 44px 'Add your first item' button; distinguish genuinely-zero from still-loading by keeping the existing Skeleton for the loading case and the EmptyState for the zero case, never reusing one for the other. Write each one to teach: 'Your closet is empty. Take a photo of one item of clothing. We will cut out the background for you.' plus a second path 'See an example closet' so a nervous user can look before committing a photo.

findings.title: Progressive disclosure: show the frequent few up front, put the rest behind ONE clearly-labelled door — never two levels deep
findings.detail: NN/g defines progressive disclosure as deferring advanced or rarely-used features to secondary screens to satisfy the conflicting needs for power and simplicity: 'Initially, show users only a few of the most important options. Offer a larger set of specialized options upon request.' Two requirements make or break it: the split must be correct (disclose everything users frequently need up front), and the progression mechanism must be obviously labelled with strong information scent so users can predict what they'll find. The hard constraint is the depth limit — 'designs going beyond 2 disclosure levels typically have low usability'. NN/g says to decide what's primary from task analysis and field studies for a new design, and from frequency-of-use statistics plus usability testing for an existing one (analytics alone can't distinguish real need from accidental visits). Staged disclosure (wizards) is the sibling pattern: it orders by workflow position rather than importance. GOV.UK's complementary rule is one thing per page — 'Asking just one question per question page helps users understand what you're asking them to do, and focus on the specific question and its answer.'
findings.actionable: Design the phase-2 'Add item' flow as staged disclosure, one question per screen: photo → category → colour → where it is stored. Everything else (brand, size, purchase price, fabric, care label, season tags, resale intent) goes behind exactly one 'Add more details (optional)' expander on a review screen — one level, never an expander inside an expander. Apply the same to the phase-4 suggestion engine: show one suggested outfit with 'Wear this' and 'Show me another', and hide the weather/occasion/recency scoring controls behind a single labelled 'Change what matters' panel. Instrument which optional fields actually get filled and promote or demote them based on real frequency rather than guesswork. Note GOV.UK's supporting evidence that the Carer's Allowance team removed a 12-step progress indicator with no negative effect on completion — don't assume a wizard needs heavy chrome.

findings.title: Default to undo, not confirmation: build a friction ladder and reserve dialogs for the genuinely irreversible
findings.detail: NN/g says designers should 'go to great lengths to provide undo' and reserve confirmation dialogs for 'actions with serious consequences — such as destroying users' work or costing large amounts of money', particularly actions that cannot be undone. The critical insight is that a confirmation dialog's effectiveness depends on its rarity: when every destructive action wears the same generic confirmation, users stop reading them and can no longer tell the reversible from the catastrophic. The practical model is a friction ladder: no confirmation → simple confirmation → explicit-consequence confirmation → type-to-confirm (NN/g cites MailChimp requiring users to type DELETE before deleting a list). Wording rules: never 'Are you sure you want to do this?' — state the actual consequence in user terms, include identifying details (the item name, the number of items, the amount) so users can spot a mistake, and label the buttons with verbs — 'Delete file' and 'Keep file', never OK/Cancel or Yes/No. NN/g separately warns against placing consequential options next to benign ones. GOV.UK restricts its warning (red) button to 'actions with serious destructive consequences that cannot be easily undone by a user. For example, permanently deleting an account' and requires a confirmation step before the final action.
findings.actionable: You already have sonner installed — use it as the undo surface. In phase 2, deleting a wardrobe item should soft-delete (add a deleted_at column to the wardrobe item model rather than a hard DELETE) and fire a toast reading 'Blue denim jacket removed' with a 44px-tall 'Undo' action, held open for at least 10 seconds (low-literacy users read slowly, so do NOT use the 4-second sonner default for anything undoable). Reserve a real dialog for exactly three acts in this product: permanently emptying the bin, transferring digital ownership on a marketplace sale, and deleting the account. Label those buttons 'Delete this item forever' / 'Keep it', and put the item name and photo inside the dialog. Keep the destructive button visually and physically separated from the benign one. Never use button.tsx's destructive variant for a reversible action.

findings.title: Flat design removes the strongest clickability signal — give tappable things borders, shadow and rectangular shape
findings.detail: NN/g's research on clickable elements opens with 'Life is too short to click on things you don't understand' — users treat clicks as currency and will not hunt for interactive elements. The strongest historical signifiers remain blue hyperlinks and rectangular buttons with a 3-D appearance; NN/g cites early research where clicks increased by 416% when a flat button was changed to a 3-D one. Concrete rules: keep the rectangular shape with rounded corners even in a flat system; never make non-clickable items (headings, status chips) look like buttons, and never use link colour or underlines for static text; avoid a page of competing colourful boxes, which destroys the signal; make the picture, icon and text of a card all clickable together to increase the effective target size; and use instantly recognisable icons, preferably with text labels, consistently across pages. Arrow icons are a weak and non-standard clickability cue.
findings.actionable: Your outline and secondary button variants in button.tsx are appropriately bordered, but the ghost variant is invisible until hover — remove ghost from any primary user path (it's currently the topbar account trigger) and keep it only for in-dialog dismissals. Give the default variant a subtle shadow-sm plus a 1px darker border so it reads as raised, and keep the existing active:translate-y-px press feedback, which is a good affordance. Critically: your dashboard currently renders non-clickable Cards (stat cards, 'Coming in the next phases' cards with border-dashed) that look exactly like the clickable item cards you'll build in phase 2. Establish and document two distinct card treatments — interactive cards get a border, hover lift and cursor-pointer with the whole card as one <a>; informational cards get no border radius change, no hover state, and a flat muted background. Also drop the font-mono 'Phase 3–4' chips: a mono chip looks like an interactive tag and says nothing to a user.

findings.title: Status must never depend on colour alone — pair every colour with an icon AND a word
findings.detail: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A) requires that colour is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element. It does not forbid colour; it requires a second channel — text, an icon, an underline, a pattern, or a change in shape or size. Roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a colour vision deficiency, and ageing further reduces colour discrimination. The two failures named most often are exactly the two your app is about to commit: status indicated by colour alone (green = clean, red = needs washing), and required fields marked only with a red asterisk. NN/g's error guidance makes the same point from the other side: put an icon beside an error message specifically to help colourblind users and improve scannability.
findings.actionable: Build D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\status-badge.tsx that structurally cannot render colour alone — its props should be {tone, icon, children} with icon and children both required, producing e.g. a check glyph + 'Clean' + green, a droplet glyph + 'In the wash' + amber, a clock glyph + 'Worn 2 days ago' + neutral. Your wardrobe domain has several colour-only traps to pre-empt: the wear-recency guardrail (don't signal 'too recently worn' with a red ring — add a text chip 'Worn on Monday'), the clean/dirty state, marketplace listing status, and borrow status. Note that badge.tsx currently defaults to h-5 with text-xs, which is too small to carry a word plus an icon — raise it to h-6/h-7 with text-sm. Also mark required form fields with the word '(required)' rather than a red asterisk, or better, follow GOV.UK and mark only the optional ones.

findings.title: Error messages: say what happened and what to DO, inline next to the field, in a summary at the top, and never in a toast
findings.detail: NN/g's ten rules for reporting form errors: validate inline as soon as the user leaves a field, not while they type (rule 7: withhold the message until they finish and exit, or premature errors frustrate); show success indicators only for genuinely complex fields like passwords; place the message adjacent to the offending field, not in a distant location; use red for errors, orange/yellow for warnings, green/blue for success, with a semi-transparent background tint on long forms; add an icon beside the message for colourblind users; keep modals for the rare case, because they force users to memorise the instruction before fixing it; never rely on a top-of-form summary alone — always pair it with field-level messages; never use tooltips for errors, because the alert icon is low-visibility and hover/focus adds cost; and when a user hits the same error three or more times, surface a link to help, because repeated failure indicates a design flaw, not a user mistake. Inline validation reduces form errors about 22% and speeds completion about 42%. GOV.UK adds the wording layer: describe what happened and how to fix it; never use technical jargon or error codes; never use 'please' (implies choice), 'sorry' (doesn't fix anything), 'valid'/'invalid', 'forbidden', 'illegal', 'you forgot', or humour like 'oops'; be specific ('Enter your first name', not 'This field is required'); use identical wording in the field-level message and the summary so it makes sense out of context; match the error to the label ('How many hours do you work a week?' → 'Enter how many hours you work a week'); use the instruction pattern for missing input ('Enter…', 'Select…') and the description pattern for constraint violations ('Name must be 35 characters or less'). Mechanically: prefix the page <title> with 'Error: ', move keyboard focus to the error summary, keep every answer the user typed, and link the message to the input with aria-describedby.
findings.actionable: This is the most urgent concrete fix in the codebase. D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\(auth)\login\page.tsx sends all failures to toast.error(getErrorMessage(error, 'Could not sign in.')) — a transient, auto-dismissing, non-specific message with no field association, which violates proximity, the no-modal/no-ephemeral principle, and the plow-reading finding (it vanishes before a slow reader finishes it). Replace it: build D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\field-error.tsx rendering an icon + red text wired via aria-describedby and aria-invalid, plus error-summary.tsx at the top of the form that receives focus on submit failure. Drop the bare HTML `required` attributes (the browser's native bubble is generic, untranslated, and transient) in favour of your own messages: 'Enter your email address', 'Enter your password'. Replace the default 'Could not sign in.' with the actionable version: 'We did not recognise that email and password. Check them and try again.' plus a 'Reset your password' link. Keep toasts only for successes and undos, never for errors.

findings.title: Skip the upfront tour: contextual help at the moment of need beats a first-run walkthrough
findings.detail: NN/g finds upfront onboarding tutorials fail for three reasons: users want to start using the product immediately and resist mandatory prep work (the paradox of the active user); information presented out of context is hard to recall when it is actually needed; and dismissing the tutorial costs effort and interrupts the task. The blunt finding is that tutorials 'don't result in better task performance'. Contextual (pull-revelation) help works instead because it fires when the user signals need. NN/g's five implementation rules: make help easy to dismiss AND easy to retrieve later; apply progressive disclosure so help is visible without overwhelming; eliminate memorisation by showing guidance alongside each step; don't explain conventional elements (a gear icon for Settings needs no coach mark); and map the user journey via research to find where help is genuinely needed. On coach marks specifically, NN/g notes they are widely abused and that users are trained to ignore them; design any instruction for scannability because users dismiss quickly, and show them when a user first encounters a feature rather than all at once.
findings.actionable: Do not build a multi-slide welcome carousel for Lumiere. Instead: (1) make the dashboard's first-run state the onboarding, using the EmptyState component from the empty-state finding as a visible 3-step checklist — 'Add your city', 'Add your first item of clothing', 'Add a photo of yourself for the fitting room' — each with a 44px button, each ticking off permanently; (2) attach one dismissible inline hint to the first genuinely novel interaction in the app, the background-removal upload ('Lay the item on a plain floor. We will remove the background.'), shown at the upload screen and not before; (3) add a persistent 'Help' entry in the same position in the sidebar and mobile nav on every screen so dismissed help is always retrievable. Do not coach-mark the search or settings icons.

findings.title: Four WCAG 2.2 criteria map directly onto features you are about to build: Consistent Help, Redundant Entry, Accessible Authentication, Dragging Movements
findings.detail: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, October 2023, and now the reference standard for ADA, Section 508 and the European Accessibility Act) added nine criteria, four of which bear directly on this product. SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A): if help is provided on multiple pages — human contact details, a contact mechanism, self-help like an FAQ, or an automated chatbot — it must appear in the same order relative to other page content across those pages. SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A): don't make users re-enter information they already gave in the same process; auto-populate or let them select it. SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum, AA): authentication must not rely on a cognitive function test — no puzzles, no object recognition, no transcription — and must not block copy-paste into password fields. SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA): any functionality operated by dragging must also be achievable with a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential. SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (AA) also matters to you specifically, because a fixed-position bottom bar is the canonical way to hide the keyboard-focused element.
findings.actionable: Four concrete actions. (1) Add a 'Help' item at a fixed position in NAV_ITEMS in D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\layout\nav-items.ts so it renders identically in both sidebar.tsx and mobile-nav.tsx on every page. (2) In the phase-2 add-item flow and phase-6 marketplace listing flow, carry forward anything already known (city, default storage location, previously used brands) rather than re-asking. (3) On login/register, never add a CAPTCHA or a picture puzzle, explicitly allow paste into the password field, and keep autoComplete="email"/"current-password" as you already have. (4) Your outfit builder and storage-location assignment must not be drag-only — pair any drag-and-drop with tap-to-select-then-tap-to-place. (5) MobileNav is `fixed inset-x-0 bottom-0 z-50`: add scroll-padding-bottom to the page container equal to the nav height so a focused input at the bottom of a long form is never hidden behind it.

findings.title: Your users are likely Urdu-first: design for 30-50% text expansion, RTL, and a language switcher named in its own language — before writing feature code
findings.detail: Localisation guidance is unanimous that this must be designed in from the start rather than retrofitted, because retrofitting is expensive and forces architectural change. Concrete rules: translated strings commonly run 30-50% longer than English, so layouts must expand and contract with content instead of being sized to the English string; Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu are the primary RTL languages (over 820 million speakers), and RTL support is more than flipping text direction — navigation patterns, icon direction and interaction flow all mirror; use CSS logical properties throughout so direction is respected automatically; mirror directional icons (back/forward arrows, progress chevrons) but do NOT mirror decorative or object icons; and numbers read left-to-right even in RTL, so don't flip '2026'. Text baked into images cannot be translated at all. This matters doubly for your audience, because a low-literacy user reading a second language is reading under two simultaneous loads.
findings.actionable: Three structural decisions to make now, while you have only 8 files. (1) D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\layout.tsx hard-codes lang="en" — move to a [locale] route segment and set both lang and dir from the locale, so adding Urdu later is config rather than surgery. (2) Replace every directional Tailwind utility with its logical equivalent across the existing components — pl-/pr-/ml-/mr-/text-left/border-l become ps-/pe-/ms-/me-/text-start/border-s; button.tsx's has-data-[icon=inline-start]:pl-2 and sidebar's px-5 are the existing offenders, and Tailwind 4 supports the logical variants natively. (3) Never truncate a label to make it fit: mobile-nav.tsx's 5 fixed flex-1 columns will break with longer translations, so plan for a 4-item nav plus 'More', and remove the `truncate` on the dashboard stat labels. Also note 'Outfit' (your chosen Google font) loads subsets:["latin"] only — it has no Arabic/Urdu coverage, so budget a Noto Nastaliq Urdu or Noto Sans Arabic fallback in the font stack now.

findings.title: Peer-reviewed low-literacy HCI research adds three patterns Western guidelines miss: voice, hand-drawn icons over photos, and a text-free path
findings.detail: A systematic review of UI design for illiterate and semi-literate users (Islam et al., Sage Open 2023) and an ACM literature review of interface guidelines for low-literature users converge on findings that go beyond WCAG and NN/g. Audio is the most-cited consideration, appearing in around 44% of the reviewed articles, covering voice input, voice output, voice information and voice-guided interfaces; the recommendation is to add speech/voice interaction alongside touch rather than instead of it. On imagery, the finding is counter-intuitive and directly actionable: low-literacy users interpret hand-drawn, figurative representations MORE successfully than photographs that contain too much detail, and far more successfully than abstract icons — so a simple line drawing of a shirt beats a photographic stock image of a shirt. Interfaces with minimal or no text, supported by graphics and audio, measurably help this group. Indrani Medhi's foundational ICTD work established the minimal-text plus audio-visual representation approach.
findings.actionable: Three additions to the Lumiere plan. (1) Add a voice layer where it is cheapest and highest-value: a microphone button beside the wardrobe search input using the Web Speech API (SpeechRecognition), so 'blue jacket' can be spoken rather than typed and spelled — this single feature removes the spelling barrier from your main retrieval path. Also expose a 'Read this to me' control on the outfit-suggestion explanation. (2) For the category icons in nav-items.ts and the phase-2 category picker, commission or pick simple figurative line drawings (Lucide is already close to this register) and avoid photographic category thumbnails; conversely, the user's OWN photos of their OWN clothes are the ideal imagery, since recognition beats reading — make the closet grid photo-first with the name as a secondary label. (3) Ensure at least one complete end-to-end path through the core task (add an item; get today's outfit) is navigable by photo, icon+label and tap alone, with no free-text entry required — make brand, notes and tags optional, never blocking.

findings.title: One primary action per screen, labelled with a verb that says what will happen
findings.detail: GOV.UK's button guidance: use sentence case describing the action performed, with 'Start now', 'Sign in', 'Continue', 'Save and continue', 'Save and come back later', 'Add another', 'Pay', 'Confirm and send' as the canonical set, adjusted for clarity ('Add another address'). Avoid multiple default (primary) buttons on a single page, since more than one primary action reduces impact and confuses users about what to do next; research cited there notes that 'pages with too many calls to action make it harder for users to know what to do next'. Secondary buttons are for secondary actions only. Don't rely on colour alone to communicate a button's function. Where user testing shows accidental double submissions, implement double-click prevention. NN/g's clickability research reinforces this from the visual side: avoid a page of competing colourful boxes, and avoid multiple calls-to-action unless clearly labelled.
findings.actionable: Give every screen in phases 2-6 exactly one default-variant button and express all other actions as outline, secondary or link. Name them with verbs from the user's vocabulary, not the system's: 'Add an item of clothing' (not 'Upload'), 'Save this outfit' (not 'Submit'), 'Show me what to wear' (not 'Generate suggestion'), 'Find where this is kept' (not 'Query storage'), 'Wear this today' (not 'Log wear'). Avoid 'Steal the Look' as a primary button label for a non-native reader — it is an idiom; keep it as the feature's name if you like the branding, but make the button itself say 'Find these clothes in my closet'. Your login page already does this well with a single full-width 'Sign in'; keep that discipline. Add double-submit protection to the login and add-item mutations.

findings.title: Purge developer jargon from user-facing copy — the dashboard currently explains JWT, Django and CORS to a wardrobe owner
findings.detail: GOV.UK's plain-English rule is mandatory for all of GOV.UK and its list of words to avoid is instructive because the offenders are abstract nouns and insider verbs: 'deliver' (use 'make', 'create', 'provide'), 'deploy' (use 'use', 'build', 'put into place'), 'facilitate' (say what you actually do), 'key' (use 'important'), 'advance' (use 'improve'). Specialist terminology must be defined at first use. WCAG 3.1.3 Unusual Words (AAA) and 3.1.4 Abbreviations (AAA) require a mechanism to explain jargon and acronyms. NN/g's rule is to use the language users use themselves. Your D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\(app)\dashboard\page.tsx ships a prominent card titled 'Foundation is live' whose body reads 'This page loaded your real account from the Django API using a JWT token, which means authentication, CORS, the database and the frontend are all talking to each other correctly' — five pieces of jargon in one 33-word sentence, which also breaks the 25-word limit. The 'Phase 3–4' / 'Phase 5' chips and 'Coming in the next phases' heading are internal roadmap language, and the UPCOMING_FEATURES bodies describe implementation ('Once the weather API and the scoring engine are wired up…').
findings.actionable: Delete the 'Foundation is live' card from the user-facing dashboard entirely — if you need it to demo the working stack to your supervisor, move it behind a /dev route or an env-gated debug panel. Rewrite UPCOMING_FEATURES to describe the user's benefit in two short sentences with no implementation detail ('See an outfit for today's weather. We pick it from clothes you already own.'). Replace the mono 'Phase 3–4' chips with 'Coming soon' or remove them. Audit all copy for the jargon list: 'wired up', 'API', 'rendered onto', 'vector search', 'embedding', 'digital ownership transfer' (say 'the item moves to their closet'), 'recency scoring' (say 'we remember what you wore recently'). For terms you genuinely must keep, define them on first use in the same sentence.

findings.title: Escalate help after repeated failure, and design the 'I'm stuck' exit on every screen
findings.detail: NN/g's tenth form-error rule is frequently skipped and is the one that most directly serves low-digital-skill users: when users encounter the same error three or more times, provide a link to support or redesign the interface, because repeated failure indicates a design flaw rather than a user mistake. This pairs with WCAG 3.2.6 Consistent Help, which covers four qualifying help types — human contact details, a human contact mechanism, self-help options, and a fully automated contact mechanism — and requires consistent relative placement. NN/g's onboarding guidance adds that dismissed help must always be retrievable.
findings.actionable: Add a failure counter to the login mutation in D:\FYP\frontend\src\hooks\use-auth.ts and to the phase-2 upload mutation: on the third identical failure, swap the inline error for an escalation block offering a different route ('Still not working? Reset your password' / 'Send us your photo and we will add it for you'). Put a single Help entry at a fixed nav position (see the WCAG 2.2 finding) and make its target a genuinely plain-language page — short sentences, one task per section, a screenshot per step — rather than a FAQ wall. For a final-year project this is also cheap marks: an escalation path is concrete evidence of inclusive design thinking.

findings.title: Encode the rules as lint rules and component APIs, not as documentation nobody reads
findings.detail: Every guideline above is a rule a future commit can silently break, and you have five more phases to build across 8 feature areas. The leverage point identified by the audit is that all the current violations live in shared primitives (button.tsx, badge.tsx, globals.css, mobile-nav.tsx, sidebar.tsx) — fixing them once propagates to every screen, whereas retrofitting later means touching every feature. NN/g's point that the low-literacy-optimised site improved outcomes for higher-literacy users too (success 46%→82%, time 22.3→9.5 minutes, satisfaction 3.5→4.4) is the argument for making the inclusive variant the ONLY variant rather than an opt-in mode — there is no expert-user cost to pay for.
findings.actionable: Make the rules mechanically enforceable. (1) Make the component API refuse the bad case: StatusBadge requires both icon and children; IconButton requires an explicit justification prop plus aria-label; EmptyState requires a primaryAction. (2) Add ESLint rules to D:\FYP\frontend\eslint.config.mjs: ban the text-[10px] / text-[11px] arbitrary-value pattern, ban h-6/h-7/h-8 and size-6/size-7/size-8 on interactive elements, ban directional spacing utilities in favour of logical ones, and flag title= on non-interactive elements. (3) Add a readability check over src/lib/copy.ts to CI. (4) Record the decisions in D:\FYP\frontend\AGENTS.md and D:\FYP\frontend\CLAUDE.md (currently 11 bytes) so every future agent-assisted change inherits them. (5) Build the whole thing as one design system with no 'simple mode' toggle — a separate accessible mode doubles your maintenance and halves the benefit.

findings.title: The onboarding cliff is the category's defining failure — not a minor annoyance
findings.detail: Every app, including the best-funded ones, loses users before value is delivered. Reviewers report "at least several days" to upload a wardrobe (Whering), "multiple hours" (Alta), and one comparison states plainly that both Indyx and Whering "only pay off after you've digitized your closet, and photographing 150 items is a real time investment that causes most people to abandon apps before delivering value." Whering's own blog implicitly concedes this by publishing a guide with six separate upload pathways. Stylebook reviewers share folk workarounds (photograph during laundry; hang items on a door with a wreath hook; use a grey sheet as backdrop) — a sign the product never solved it.
findings.actionable: Treat time-to-first-value as the primary product metric, not catalog completeness. Ship a flow that delivers a real answer after ~10 items (e.g. "where are my black jeans" / one suggestion), and never gate the app behind a completed wardrobe. Put a visible "you can add more later" escape on every add screen, and design the app so a 30-item partial closet is genuinely useful.

findings.title: Copy Whering's multi-path ingestion and bulk multi-select + mass-tagging
findings.detail: Whering offers six add paths: long-press any web image → share sheet → Whering; an in-app web capture/crop browser; a community-uploaded item database to match pieces you own; a pre-populated "Whering Basics" starter set; camera roll multi-select (up to 15 images at once, each becoming an item); and in-app camera. Crucially, tagging is decoupled from capture: after upload you "long press on an item, select as many as you like" and apply tags, seasons or brands in bulk. Indyx lets users forward shopping receipts for automatic entry and scans receipts; Acloset imports retail order history (Amazon, Zara) and has a "Smart Detector" that converts mirror selfies into clean product images.
findings.actionable: Build capture-now/tag-later as the core architecture: camera roll multi-select (15–20 at a time), then a bulk-edit mode driven by long-press multi-select where one gesture assigns category, season, and — your differentiator — storage location to 20 items at once. Assigning location in bulk while standing in front of one drawer is dramatically cheaper than per-item entry; make that the hero onboarding flow.

findings.title: Auto-tagging accuracy is the #1 trust killer; plan for cheap correction, not perfect AI
findings.detail: A Whering App Store reviewer says the app's guesses about style and colour are "correct about 50% of the time"; others report "nonsensical tags", a bug where auto-added tags duplicate instead of deleting, and cardigans classified as shirts/outerwear rather than sweaters. Acloset reviewers hit the same cardigan misclassification and call the AI analysis "slow and inaccurate." Wrong tags then poison downstream suggestions — one analysis notes "wrong tagging can result in mismatched pairings like a blazer with athletic shorts."
findings.actionable: Show auto-tags as editable chips with confidence, correctable in one tap from the grid (no drill-into-detail-screen required), and never let a low-confidence tag silently drive a suggestion. Keep your taxonomy small and unambiguous where competitors fail (layer role: base / mid / outer, not "sweater vs outerwear"). Log corrections and re-use them as training signal per-user.

findings.title: Background removal fails often enough to be a named complaint in every app
findings.detail: Whering: "background remover... sometimes picks up things little things from the background." Stylebook's tool "has some trouble getting the lines just right automatically" even on contrasting backgrounds, and its iPad manual tool has edge-detection bugs. Cladwell "claims automatic background removal but struggled to get it to work properly." Pureple's is manual and "quite buggy and can take a few tries." Acloset's upload is "glitchy and may require more than one attempt." SimpleCloset requires manual cutout per item. Only Fits and Indyx are praised here.
findings.actionable: Use the on-device iOS 17+ subject-lift / VisionKit path as primary (SimpleCloset already does) with a server model as fallback, and always ship a fast manual lasso. Make cutout optional and non-blocking: accept the raw photo, queue the cutout, and never make a failed cutout stop an item from being saved. Do not make a beautiful flatlay a precondition for inventory.

findings.title: Closet grid: thumbnails are too small and dark colours are indistinguishable
findings.detail: Stylebook reviewers say icons are "far too small on the iPhone," making it hard to tell grey from navy from black, and ask for adjustable default grid sizes and larger text on category screens. Cladwell gets the identical complaint: "poor photo rendering; navy and black items appear identical," plus item names are absent from outfit suggestions so users can't identify which piece is meant. Indyx paywalls its "birds-eye view" density control behind a $60/yr membership, which one reviewer names as the single feature they most want in the free tier. Save Your Wardrobe has the opposite defect: "picture boxes for clothes are far too big and often crop images weirdly."
findings.actionable: Ship a free, persistent grid-density toggle (2/3/4/5 across) and put a colour-swatch dot plus a short text label on each card so near-blacks are separable. Item card should carry: thumbnail, colour swatch, and one contextual line that you can make your differentiator — the storage location ("Top drawer") or state ("in wash"). Never paywall display density.

findings.title: Organization models worth copying: two-level folders, custom tags, and item status
findings.detail: Stylebook has a "two-level closet category system with folders and subcategories" that users can add/edit/delete/reorder, 100+ colour shades per item, and — most relevant to you — filter by item status: clean, laundry, cleaners, lent out, wishlist. Fits lets users "create your own tags with custom colors and emojis." SimpleCloset is "highly customizable" with reorderable properties, multiple closets, and a "memory box" to archive rather than delete items. Indyx uses "Collections" as user-defined groupings (Activewear, packing lists).
findings.actionable: Adopt Stylebook's status field and merge it with your location model — clean/laundry/at the cleaners/lent out/packed are all just *locations* in a unified place graph. That unification is a genuinely novel product idea and it makes location data self-maintaining, because users already want to log "it's in the wash." Also copy the archive-not-delete pattern; deletion anxiety is real in wardrobe apps.

findings.title: Filtering and search are weak almost everywhere — a cheap place to win
findings.detail: A 10-app feature matrix shows only GetWardrobe and Fits with anything beyond "basic" filters; Acloset, Whering and Indyx are marked as having no advanced filters at all, and GetWardrobe paywalls AND/OR logic as Premium. Concrete failures: Stylebook users cannot search brands already entered and must scroll and manually select; Acloset users can't search preloaded items; Whering users report "difficulty filtering by garment type during outfit creation." Indyx's search does filter the closet view live as you type a brand/keyword/style — the one good implementation cited.
findings.actionable: Make search first-class and free: live-filtering as-you-type (Indyx pattern) over name, brand, colour, tag AND location, with compound filters ("navy + in the wash + location: hall closet"). Critically, expose filters *inside* the outfit builder, which is exactly where Whering users complain they're missing. Cheap to build, repeatedly requested, rarely done well.

findings.title: Four distinct outfit-builder patterns exist; pick by job, don't copy blindly
findings.detail: (1) Free-form canvas collage — Stylebook ("magazine-style outfits on a free-form canvas" with pinch/drag, Outfit Shuffle, clone-to-variant), Pureple drag-and-drop, SimpleCloset drag-and-drop, GetWardrobe drag-drop canvas, Combyne "nice canvas editor." (2) Category slot columns + shuffle — Whering's Styling tab, explicitly compared to "Cher's iconic outfit generator in Clueless," with fixed slot templates (one-piece+shoes; top+bottom+shoes; +outer); Cladwell similar. (3) Mannequin dressing room with swipe — Fits lets you "dress a virtual mannequin and swipe through your closet." (4) AI auto-layout — Acloset Layout auto-generates a complete outfit including accessories, then you refine by excluding items.
findings.actionable: Build tap-to-select slot columns with filters as the default (fast, thumb-friendly, good for your context-aware angle) and offer free-form canvas only as an optional "style it" mode. Canvas manipulation is where the worst interaction bugs live, so don't make it the critical path. Always include clone-an-outfit-to-variant (Stylebook) — it's the cheapest way to grow outfit count.

findings.title: Specific outfit-builder defects to avoid, copied from real reviews
findings.detail: Stylebook: the manual resize slider is "unresponsive unless you touch at the exact right spot"; pinch-to-zoom requires multiple manual resizes; no landscape rotation; no iPad/desktop version. Cladwell: hard cap of 4 items per outfit (one must be shoes), no accessories in suggestions, and you cannot layer two items in the same category (e.g. leggings under a dress) — a structural modelling error. Acloset: no way to group or categorize saved outfits, so a user with 292 outfits must scroll all of them; shoes lump heels with flats; only one jewellery item allowed. Whering: calendar view is hard to read because the date overlay sits on the outfit.
findings.actionable: Design the outfit data model with unlimited items, multiple items per slot, and an explicit layer order from day one — retrofitting this is what broke Cladwell. Add outfit collections/folders before users pass ~50 outfits. Use generous hit targets for canvas handles, and support landscape/tablet. Keep calendar thumbnails unobstructed by date chrome.

findings.title: Wear-logging friction quietly kills the data your suggestions depend on
findings.detail: A Stylebook reviewer states it takes "too many clicks/touches to quickly log a look on the calendar," and asks to add looks directly to packing lists, reorder items within lists, and mark items as actually worn for future reference. Every app's headline analytics (cost-per-wear, "forgotten items", wear streaks) are only as good as this logging loop, and cost-per-wear is the single most praised feature across Whering, Cladwell, Acloset and Stylebook reviews.
findings.actionable: Make "I wore this" a one-tap action from the home screen and from a notification, with no confirmation dialog, and auto-transition the item's location to "laundry" on log. That single coupling gives you wear data and location freshness from one tap — the highest-leverage interaction in your product.

findings.title: AI suggestion quality is the most consistent disappointment across all apps
findings.detail: Cladwell: "A leather jacket with an open front blazer and no pants? An outfit with TWO blazers?", heavy layers recommended in 97°F heat, the same combos repeatedly, over-reliance on cardigans in all seasons. Acloset: "a turtleneck sweater with a sweater dress", "nonsensical outfit pairings" with "the same items consistently restyled" while ignoring other parts of the closet. Whering: "AI feature results often feel random and disconnected from personal style"; randomly generated suggestions "often unwearable." Pureple: "most outfits don't quite go together" and it "seems to completely ignore some of the clothes." Users also say they can't permanently reject a suggestion. The one good mechanic: Acloset learns from rejections — mark a pairing as "mismatched categories" and it stops pairing those items.
findings.actionable: Ship explicit, persistent negative feedback ("never pair these", "retire this item from suggestions") and a coverage guarantee that rotates in under-used items. State the reason for each suggestion ("7°C and you have a 9am client meeting") — explainability converts a weird suggestion from a bug into a negotiation. Prefer fewer, defensible suggestions over an infinite shuffle.

findings.title: Context-aware suggestion is no longer a gap — Alta already owns the obvious version
findings.detail: Alta Daily generates daily outfits from your calendar, the weather, and your style; it was named a TIME Best Invention of 2025, has a CFDA partnership, is free, and sits at 4.9/5 across ~14K ratings, with reviewers praising rediscovery ("I'm wearing clothes I haven't worn in a while") and a "weirdly very accurate" try-on avatar. Acloset suggests by schedule, weather and mood with a user-set "sensible temperature" for personal heat tolerance; Clueless auto-plans a full week every Sunday; Cladwell does daily weather-aware suggestions plus ChatGPT integration.
findings.actionable: Do not position on "context-aware suggestions" generically — you will be compared to a TIME-award app with 4.9 stars and lose. Position on the context nobody models: physical accessibility. "Suggest outfits from what is clean, unpacked, and reachable right now" (excluding the vacuum-bagged winter bin in the loft and the shirt at the dry cleaner) is a defensible claim that only your location graph can make.

findings.title: Physical storage location DOES already exist — but only as a dead metadata field
findings.detail: This is the most important correction to your premise. Indyx's App Store description states you can "add brand, season, location, and more — and, filter or search across your entire wardrobe by any of the above", where location means where the item is stored. SimpleCloset has first-class "storage locations" and in v2.20.0 (Apr 2025) added "Support filtering storage locations on the random outfits page." Acloset's add-item form includes "locations" among material/occasion attributes. A tiny unrated app, Closet Organizer Pro (first released Feb 2025, "hasn't received enough ratings"), goes furthest: its listing says "Photograph your actual wardrobe and the app maps its shelves and compartments, so you always know where everything is," with drawer/storage-box support and periodic location-confirmation reminders. Stylebook has no field at all — and a reviewer invented the workaround of "label its location in the notes" (dresser vs closet) for faster outfit planning.
findings.actionable: Stop claiming location tracking is absent — claim that it is unbuilt. Everywhere it exists it's a flat, optional, typed string with no visual model, no put-away flow, no retrieval flow, and no effect on suggestions (SimpleCloset's one integration is a filter on a random-outfit page). Your differentiator must be the closed loop, not the field. Also treat Closet Organizer Pro as your nearest competitor and install it before you build.

findings.title: The adjacent storage-inventory category has already solved location UX — copy it wholesale
findings.detail: Sortly (home inventory) uses custom nested folders/subfolders by location, tracks items as they move between locations, and generates printable QR/barcode labels "so you know exactly what's in that box without having to open it." Codenize models sites → locations → bins → items, gives each bin a permanent QR code, has a live camera scanner, a "move item" function to reorganize digitally, and "search once across all bins to find exactly where everything is stored." BoxQR: name a bin, get a QR, add contents by typing OR photos OR AI image recognition that "scans the image and lists what it sees", printable PDF label sheets, "Browse by Location, Move in Bulk." Storage Box Organizer emphasizes "snap photos as you pack with no typing needed." None of these know anything about outfits, colour, season, or styling.
findings.actionable: Lift three mechanics directly: (1) a nested location hierarchy (room → furniture → drawer/shelf/bin) rather than a free-text field; (2) printable QR labels on drawers and seasonal bins, so scanning a drawer opens its contents and scanning during put-away sets location in bulk; (3) an explicit "move" action with bulk select for seasonal rotation. Your wedge is that you are the only product that will own both the place graph and the outfit graph.

findings.title: Your real gap: no app answers "where is it" or "what can I actually reach today"
findings.detail: Synthesis across every source: wardrobe apps are built as catalogues and styling toys, not as retrieval systems. They optimize for looking at your closet (Acloset is "more about looking at your wardrobe beautifully than optimizing how you use it") and for analytics. Meanwhile the recurring user job is retrieval and memory: reviewers describe the core value as rediscovering forgotten items, one credits the app with managing ADHD-related clothing chaos, and commentary on neurodivergent wardrobe use frames the problem as object permanence — "an object out of sight is forgotten." Nobody has built put-away, find-it, or seasonal-rotation flows on top of that.
findings.actionable: Build three flows no competitor has: (a) Find it — search/tap an item, get "Bedroom → tall dresser → 2nd drawer" plus a photo of the drawer; (b) Put it away — after laundry, bulk-assign items back to locations in one screen, with scan-a-QR shortcut; (c) Rotate — seasonal swap wizard that moves a filtered set to/from storage bins and flags items still marked as in the loft when you've "worn" them. Target the ADHD/object-permanence and small-home/multi-location-storage audiences explicitly — they have the pain and nobody markets retrieval to them.

findings.title: Monetization: item caps and subscriptions generate the angriest reviews
findings.detail: Acloset reviewers: "To make someone pay annually, monthly or weekly just to use your simple app… absurdity", with long-term users abandoning over cost and asking for one-time purchase; free tier caps at 100 items. GetWardrobe also caps free at 100. Pureple's free tier is limited and it's criticized for "annoying and incessant pop-up ads" plus paywalled AI outfits. Cladwell users question $60/yr value "amid limited recent improvements" and limit free use to one outfit a day. A Whering reviewer begs for "one-time fee (PLEASE no subscriptions!!)". The loved counter-examples are Stylebook at a $4.99 one-time price and SimpleCloset at ~$10 one-time; Whering and Alta are free.
findings.actionable: Never cap item count — it punishes exactly the data entry you're asking users to do, and it's the most-resented paywall in the category. Keep unlimited items, unlimited locations, and search free; charge for a one-time unlock or a modest subscription tied to genuinely optional value (printable QR label packs, multi-home/household sharing, advanced analytics). Avoid ads entirely.

findings.title: Offline, backup, sync and export are widely broken — and they matter more for you
findings.detail: An Indyx reviewer found "app did not load without a connection" on a flight, in a product whose main use case includes packing. Smart Closet reportedly has "no real way to back up your closet" and crashes when creating a look or adding to the calendar. Stylebook has no cloud sync and no account system, so data is device-bound and stats can't follow you across devices — a long-standing complaint. In a 10-app matrix, only Stylebook and GetWardrobe offer offline modes and only GetWardrobe offers data export (CSV + image ZIP); SimpleCloset offers Excel export and iCloud backup.
findings.actionable: Make the app fully offline-first and local-first: a user standing in a walk-in closet or a basement storage unit frequently has no signal, and a "where is it" feature that fails offline is worthless. Ship iCloud/Drive backup and CSV+image export from v1 — it's rare enough to be a trust differentiator and it de-risks the hours of data entry you're asking for.

findings.title: Repeatedly requested features that still don't exist across the category
findings.detail: Compiled from App Store reviews: quantity/duplicates for the same item in multiple colours; gift status and year-purchased fields; permanent rejection of a suggestion; outfit grouping/collections once counts grow; random outfit restricted to a chosen category; uploading multiple photos per item (Whering explicitly allows only one); a photo of the outfit as actually worn on your body so the AI learns fit; hairstyle/accessory completeness; 12-hour clock and default size/country settings; full iPad/landscape support (Stylebook, Whering); inspiration-photo-driven outfit building (Acloset); packing-list improvements (add a look directly, reorder within the list, mark what was actually worn).
findings.actionable: Cheap high-signal wins for your v1 backlog: multiple photos per item (including a photo of the drawer/bin it lives in — dual purpose for you), quantity/duplicate handling, outfit collections, per-category randomizer, "never suggest again", and iPad support. Multi-photo and packing-list-with-locations are natural extensions of your location model rather than bolt-ons.

findings.title: The academic evidence tells you which outcomes to market
findings.detail: A peer-reviewed study in Sustainability (Jiang & Macintyre, Heriot-Watt, May 2025) content-analysed 27 wardrobe management apps and thematically analysed all 5,953 Apple and Google Play reviews. It found ~470 users reporting behavioural shifts — reduced overconsumption and increased garment utilisation — and ~210 describing psychological benefits such as improved mental clarity and reduced anxiety. Review-derived anecdotes match: one Whering user's monthly clothing spend dropped from ~$400 to ~$50.
findings.actionable: Market outcomes, not inventory: "stop re-buying what you own", "calmer mornings", "find it in seconds". Instrument these as in-app metrics (items rediscovered after N months in storage, time-to-find, duplicate-purchase warnings triggered) so your location data produces a measurable claim competitors cannot make. Cite this study in any academic write-up of your FYP.

findings.title: Sources to treat with caution — much of the "comparison" content is competitor marketing
findings.detail: The richest comparison pages are published by competing apps: myindyx.com/blog and /versus pages are Indyx's, getwardrobe.com/compare is GetWardrobe's feature matrix (unsurprisingly scoring itself highest), clueless.clothing, vestatheapp.com, fits-app.com, nouva.app, outflik.com and stylepal.app all sell competing products. Grokipedia is LLM-generated. Kimola, MDPI, ideas.repec and justuseapp/appgrooves were partly inaccessible (403/410/DNS), and Reddit is not fetchable by this agent at all, so direct Reddit threads could not be quoted.
findings.actionable: Before finalising your FYP literature/competitor chapter, verify the feature matrices yourself by installing Indyx, SimpleCloset, Closet Organizer Pro, Whering and Alta and recording the actual add-item and location flows with screenshots — first-party marketing is not a citable competitive analysis. For the Reddit voice-of-customer you wanted, run manual searches in r/femalefashionadvice, r/ADHD, r/declutter and r/ThriftStoreHauls and quote threads directly.

summary: Across Whering, Acloset, Stylebook, Cladwell, Indyx, Save Your Wardrobe, Pureple, Smart Closet, Alta and several newcomers, the category has one universal failure (the onboarding data-entry cliff — multi-day uploads that cause most users to abandon before value) and one universal disappointment (AI outfit suggestions that repeat, ignore large parts of the closet, and produce nonsensical pairings). Everything else users complain about is mundane and fixable: unreliable background removal, ~50%-accurate auto-tags, thumbnails too small to tell navy from black, search that can't even find brands you already typed, filters missing exactly where you need them (inside the outfit builder), too many taps to log a wear, item-count paywalls, no offline mode, no export, no backup. IMPORTANT CORRECTION to your premise: physical storage location is NOT absent. Indyx has a filterable "location" field, SimpleCloset has first-class "storage locations," Acloset has a "locations" attribute, and a tiny unrated app (Closet Organizer Pro, Feb 2025) claims to map your wardrobe's shelves and compartments — while Stylebook users hack it into the notes field. But in every case it is a dead, flat, optional string with no visual place model, no put-away flow, no find-it flow, no seasonal rotation, and essentially no effect on suggestions. Meanwhile an entirely separate category (Sortly, Codenize, BoxQR, Storage Box Organizer) has already solved location UX properly — nested room→furniture→bin hierarchies, permanent QR labels, bulk "move," photo-first capture with no typing — and knows nothing about clothes. Your defensible wedge is therefore the closed loop, not the field: own both the place graph and the outfit graph, and position on physical accessibility ("what's clean, unpacked and reachable right now") rather than generic context-awareness, because Alta already owns generic context-awareness with a TIME Best Invention award and 4.9/5 from ~14K ratings. Copy Whering's multi-path ingestion plus long-press bulk tagging (extend it to bulk location assignment — the killer onboarding flow), Stylebook's two-level folders and clean/laundry/cleaners/lent-out status (unify status WITH location so the data self-maintains), Indyx's live-filtering search, and Sortly/Codenize's QR + move mechanics. Avoid item caps, ads, canvas-first outfit editing, 4-item outfit models that can't layer, and any online-only behaviour.

Researched production DRF patterns against the actual Lumiere codebase (Django 5.2, DRF 3.16, psycopg 3.2, Neon, Cloudinary, rembg, pgvector planned). The architecture is already above average for an FYP — per-feature apps, owner-scoped querysets everywhere, deliberate denormalisation of wear_count/last_worn_date, composite indexes, separate list/detail serializers. Nine concrete defects or gaps were found that will bite as the project grows into Phases 4-6. The three most urgent: (1) CONN_MAX_AGE=600 with no CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS against a Neon compute that autosuspends after 300s will throw OperationalError on reused dead connections — a guaranteed production failure, not a maybe; (2) StorageLocation.full_path / ancestors / descendant_ids each walk the parent/child chain with one query per level, so the closet grid and the ?location= filter are N+1 (and the existing select_related only covers one of four possible levels); (3) the image upload path calls Image.open().load() on attacker-controlled bytes before any pixel-dimension check, and trusts the client-supplied Content-Type — Pillow's default only *warns* up to 89M pixels and only errors above 178M (~715 MB of RGBA), so a 12 MB PNG can OOM-kill the worker. Also flagged: no API versioning (cheapest to fix now, before the Next.js client hardcodes paths); no throttling in front of paid fal.ai/OpenWeather calls; the SQLite fallback means tests never exercise ArrayField/GIN/pgvector and a missing DATABASE_URL boots production silently; missing (owner, -created_at) index for the default list ordering; ArrayField contains and SearchFilter icontains both unindexed, with the icontains case having a well-known trap where a plain gin_trgm_ops index is silently ignored. For background work, Django 6.0's django.tasks (available today as the django-tasks backport with a DatabaseBackend worker) is now the idiomatic no-Celery path and is a better answer than threads-in-request; the hard line where synchronous stops being acceptable is rembg, which pins a 176 MB model resident per gunicorn worker and blocks it for seconds.

findings.title: CONN_MAX_AGE=600 against Neon's 300s autosuspend will throw OperationalError — add CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS
findings.detail: config/settings.py sets DATABASES["default"]["CONN_MAX_AGE"] = 600 with no CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS. Neon suspends the compute after 300 seconds of inactivity (always on, not disableable on the Free plan), and Neon's own docs name the symptom: "terminating connection due to administrator command ... typically encountered when running a query from a connection that has sat idle long enough for the compute to suspend." Django's docs state the rule directly: "If your database terminates idle connections after some time, you should set CONN_MAX_AGE to a lower value, so that Django doesn't attempt to use a connection that has been terminated by the database server." CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS=True (Django 4.1+) "can be used to improve the robustness of connection reuse and prevent errors when a connection has been closed by the database server" — it costs one cheap liveness check per request, only when the DB is actually touched. A 600s max age in front of a 300s idle kill is the exact inverse of what you want: every first request after a quiet spell hits a corpse.
findings.actionable: In config/settings.py: set CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS = True, and drop CONN_MAX_AGE to 120 (well under Neon's 300s suspend window) or 0 if you move to ASGI. Keep both as env-tunable so Render/production can differ from local. Then verify by leaving the app idle 6+ minutes and hitting /api/wardrobe/items/ — it should succeed, not 500.

findings.title: If you use Neon's -pooler endpoint, DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS is mandatory, and migrations must bypass it
findings.detail: Neon's pooled endpoint is PgBouncer in transaction mode. Django's docs are unambiguous: "Using a connection pooler in transaction pooling mode (e.g. PgBouncer) requires disabling server-side cursors for that connection" — because server-side cursors are connection-local and survive past a transaction when AUTOCOMMIT is True, so a later transaction landing on a different pooled backend raises. Django uses server-side cursors for QuerySet.iterator(), which you will reach for the moment you batch-embed the wardrobe for pgvector. Neon additionally lists what transaction mode cannot do: SET/RESET, LISTEN/NOTIFY, SQL-level PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, WITH HOLD cursors, session-level advisory locks. Two non-obvious good-news items: protocol-level prepared statements *are* supported by Neon's PgBouncer, and Django already defaults to client-side binding with psycopg 3.1.8+, so you are safe unless someone sets server_side_binding: True — don't. Finally, Neon says to use the *direct* endpoint for schema migrations and admin scripts; CREATE EXTENSION vector and an HNSW index build both want a real session.
findings.actionable: Decide explicitly which endpoint DATABASE_URL points at. If it has -pooler: add DATABASES["default"]["DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS"] = True, and add a second env var (e.g. DATABASE_URL_DIRECT) used by a DATABASES["direct"] alias for `migrate` and the pgvector extension/index migrations. Never set OPTIONS["server_side_binding"] = True. Document the choice in .env.example next to the DATABASE_URL comment.

findings.title: Don't add a second pool layer (OPTIONS pool) on top of Neon's PgBouncer — and know it is mutually exclusive with CONN_MAX_AGE
findings.detail: Django 5.1+ supports a native psycopg3 pool via OPTIONS: {"pool": True} (needs psycopg[pool]). It is tempting but wrong here for three reasons. First, it is mutually exclusive with persistent connections — the pool requires CONN_MAX_AGE = 0, so you cannot have both. Second, Neon already fronts the database with PgBouncer accepting up to 10,000 client connections with default_pool_size at 90% of max_connections; a per-gunicorn-worker pool on top of that is a third layer of queueing for no throughput gain at FYP scale. Third and most concrete for a student budget: a pool that keeps min_size>0 idle connections open holds the Neon compute awake and defeats scale-to-zero, which is what keeps the free tier free. Separately, Django's docs warn that "when using ASGI, persistent connections should be disabled" — so if Phase 5 pushes you to async views for the fal.ai calls, CONN_MAX_AGE must go to 0 at the same time.
findings.actionable: Stay on CONN_MAX_AGE (lowered, with health checks) for now and do not add OPTIONS pool. Write the ASGI coupling into a comment in settings.py next to CONN_MAX_AGE so the Phase 5 async work doesn't silently break connection handling. Revisit pooling only if you move off Neon or disable scale-to-zero on a paid plan.

findings.title: StorageLocation tree walking is N+1 three separate ways — fix all three with a materialized path
findings.detail: apps/wardrobe/models.py has three methods that each issue one query per tree level, and all three are on hot paths. (1) `ancestors` walks `node = node.parent` in a loop, and `full_path` calls it — StorageLocationSerializer exposes full_path and depth on every list response, but StorageLocationViewSet only does .select_related("parent"), so a depth-3 drawer costs 2 extra queries per row. (2) GarmentItem.location_path calls storage_location.full_path; GarmentItemViewSet selects storage_location__parent only — one level of a MAX_DEPTH=4 tree — so a page of 24 items stored in drawers costs up to 48 extra queries. (3) descendant_ids() does stack.extend(node.children.all()) — one query per node — and GarmentItemFilter.filter_location calls it on every ?location= request, as does the /locations/{id}/items/ action. The /tree/ action's prefetch_related("children__children__children") is the hardcoded-depth symptom of the same problem. A materialized path column (e.g. `path = CharField` holding "3.7.12", plus a cached `depth`) collapses all three: full_path becomes a single prefetch or a denormalised `path_names`, and descendant_ids becomes `filter(path__startswith=f"{self.path}.")` — one indexed query instead of O(nodes). You are already comfortable denormalising (wear_count/last_worn_date on GarmentItem, with a good comment explaining why), so this is consistent with the project's own stated reasoning.
findings.actionable: Add `path` (indexed CharField) and `depth` (PositiveSmallIntegerField) to StorageLocation, maintained in a `storage_location_create`/`storage_location_move` service that recomputes descendants inside transaction.atomic(). Rewrite descendant_ids() to use path__startswith, and full_path to read from a denormalised path_names field or a single .select_related chain. Delete the children__children__children prefetch. Guard it with an assertNumQueries test on /api/wardrobe/items/?location=N so it cannot regress.

findings.title: Image upload trusts client Content-Type and decodes before checking dimensions — decompression-bomb and OOM risk
findings.detail: GarmentImageUploadView checks upload.size > 12 MB and then `content_type = upload.content_type`, which is supplied by the client in the multipart part header and is trivially forged. The real decode happens in apps/vision/background.py: `source = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes)); source.load()` with no pixel-count check in between. I read the installed Pillow 11.3: MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS defaults to 89,478,485 and `_decompression_bomb_check` only emits a *warning* at that threshold — it raises DecompressionBombError solely above 2× that, i.e. 178,956,970 pixels, roughly 715 MB as RGBA. So a compliant, under-12 MB, highly-compressed PNG can legitimately expand to hundreds of MB inside your web worker, which on a small Render instance is an OOM kill, not an exception you can catch. Django's security doc confirms the type-sniffing half: "an HTML file can be uploaded as an image if that file contains a valid PNG header followed by malicious HTML. This file will pass verification of the library that Django uses for ImageField image processing (Pillow)." Two things you already do right and should keep: you re-encode to PNG server-side (which destroys polyglot payloads in the cutout), and you serve from Cloudinary's own domain, which satisfies Django's "always serving user uploaded content from a distinct top-level or second-level domain" advice — say that in the thesis. One real bug: ALLOWED_IMAGE_TYPES includes image/heic and image/heif, but Pillow cannot open HEIC without pillow-heif, so an iPhone upload passes your allowlist and then dies as "That file is not a readable image."
findings.actionable: In background.py: set Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS explicitly (e.g. 40_000_000), then after Image.open() — which reads only the header — check source.size against a max like 8000x8000 and reject BEFORE calling .load().
