In views.py: derive the format from the decoded image (source.format) rather than upload.content_type, and use content_type only as a cheap pre-filter. Either add pillow-heif to requirements/base.txt or drop heic/heif from ALLOWED_IMAGE_TYPES. Also set DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE / FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE in settings and cap body size at the proxy, as Django's security doc advises.

findings.title: rembg in the request cycle is the line where synchronous stops being acceptable — use django.tasks / django-tasks, not threads
findings.detail: Your own comment in background.py says the u2net model is ~176 MB and is cached in a module global so it is not reloaded per request. That is the right call for one worker and the wrong shape for several: each gunicorn worker process gets its own copy, so 2-3 workers is ~350-530 MB resident before any request arrives, and the first request per worker also blocks while downloading it. Each removal then blocks that worker for seconds, against gunicorn's default 30s timeout. That is the concrete threshold: CPU-bound, multi-second, memory-heavy work in a sync worker is where you must move off the request cycle. For the no-Celery path, the answer changed recently — Django 6.0 shipped a first-party Tasks framework in django.tasks with a @task decorator, a TASKS setting, and Task.enqueue(), explicitly for "running code outside the HTTP request-response cycle." The important caveat, repeated by every reviewer: it ships only ImmediateBackend and DummyBackend and deliberately includes no worker, no scheduling, no retries, no persistence — the core team chose not to ship a database-backed worker. The reference implementation with a real DatabaseBackend and a worker management command is the `django-tasks` package, which is also a backport, so on Django 5.2 you can adopt the exact API today and the move to Django 6.x becomes a settings change. Avoid the threads-in-request alternative: a thread spawned in a view outlives the response, is killed arbitrarily on worker recycle, and leaks DB connections unless you call django.db.close_old_connections() yourself. Async views are not the fix either — the work is CPU-bound, so an event loop buys nothing, and DRF needs adrf for async views anyway.
findings.actionable: Install django-tasks, configure TASKS with the DatabaseBackend, and move remove_background + the two Cloudinary uploads into a task enqueued from the upload endpoint. Return 202 with a job id; have the Add Item page poll a small status endpoint (you already split upload from item creation, so the UI shape is right). Run the worker as a second Render process. Keep the synchronous path behind a setting so local dev and the demo stay single-process. Do the same for fal.ai try-on in Phase 5, which is the other multi-second call.

findings.title: No API versioning yet — fix it now, before the Next.js client hardcodes /api/wardrobe/
findings.detail: config/urls.py mounts everything at /api/<app>/ and REST_FRAMEWORK sets no DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS, so request.version does not exist and there is no way to change a response shape without breaking the frontend. This is the cheapest item on this list today and one of the most expensive in Phase 6, when the marketplace starts reshaping GarmentItem payloads. DRF's own guidance: AcceptHeaderVersioning is "generally considered as best practice", URLPathVersioning suits "small ad-hoc projects", and NamespaceVersioning is "probably easier to manage for larger projects". For a decoupled Next.js client and a thesis examiner reading Swagger, a path version wins on legibility — an Accept-header version is invisible in the docs page and in the browser. The documented caveat to respect: always pass request into reverse() (reverse('x', request=request)) and into hyperlinked serializer context, or generated URLs lose the version.
findings.actionable: Move the feature includes under path("api/v1/", ...) in config/urls.py, set DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS to rest_framework.versioning.NamespaceVersioning (or URLPathVersioning) with DEFAULT_VERSION="v1" and ALLOWED_VERSIONS=["v1"], and update NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL usage in frontend/src/lib. Keep /api/health/ unversioned. Check drf-spectacular still generates one clean schema (it may need SERVE_URLCONF or a per-version schema view).

findings.title: Pagination: keep page numbers for the closet grid, move to cursor for append-only feeds — and add a unique tiebreaker
findings.detail: Current config is PageNumberPagination with PAGE_SIZE=24, which is the right default for the closet grid: users want page numbers and a total count, and a personal wardrobe is hundreds of rows, where OFFSET is free. The cost to know about is the COUNT(*) every page issues, plus the fact that offset pagination "forces the database to scan and discard rows before returning results" and is "inherently racy with live data" — insert between page 1 and 2 and an item is skipped, delete and one is duplicated. The places that will actually hurt are the Phase 3 wear log, the Phase 5 similarity results, and the Phase 6 marketplace feed: append-heavy, infinite-scroll, multi-user. DRF ships CursorPagination for exactly this, with constant cost at any depth. The trap specific to your models: GarmentItem.Meta.ordering is ["-created_at"] and created_at is not unique, so cursor pagination over it can skip or repeat rows at page boundaries — cursor pagination needs a total order.
findings.actionable: Keep PageNumberPagination as the global default. Add a project CursorPagination subclass (ordering = ("-created_at", "-id"), page_size=24, max_page_size capped) and set pagination_class on the wear-log, marketplace and similarity-search viewsets as you build them. Change GarmentItem.Meta.ordering and the viewset's ordering to ("-created_at", "-id") now so the tiebreaker exists everywhere. Never expose an unbounded page_size_query_param.

findings.title: Index gaps on the list endpoint: missing (owner, -created_at), unindexed ArrayField contains, and a trgm index that will be silently ignored
findings.detail: GarmentItem declares four composite indexes — (owner,status), (owner,category), (owner,last_worn_date), (owner,storage_location) — but the default list query is filter(owner=...) ORDER BY -created_at, and no index covers it, so Postgres must sort every time. Column order matters and should "reflect your query's filter funnel, starting with the column that eliminates the most rows fastest" — owner first, then the sort key. Two filters are entirely unindexable as written: filter_season and filter_occasion use ArrayField `contains`, and Django's docs note db_index/Index create a B-tree which "isn't particularly helpful when querying complex data types" — arrays want GinIndex. The third is the one that catches almost everyone: SearchFilter over name/brand/notes/category__name generates `UPPER(col::text) LIKE UPPER('%q%')`, and a plain gin_trgm_ops index is built for ILIKE, so the planner cannot use it and you get a sequential scan — Django ticket #32803 documents exactly this, with measured 368ms vs 1.5ms. The index has to match the expression Django actually emits.
findings.actionable: Add to GarmentItem.Meta.indexes: Index(fields=["owner","-created_at"]) (and consider a partial version with condition=Q(status="IN_WARDROBE") since the grid almost always filters to wearable); GinIndex(fields=["seasons"]) and GinIndex(fields=["occasions"]). For search, add a TrigramExtension() migration and index the emitted expression — GinIndex(OpClass(Upper("name"), name="gin_trgm_ops"), name="garment_name_trgm") — or switch to a SearchVectorField + GinIndex and drop SearchFilter. Verify each with EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than assuming; trim ordering_fields to the sorts the UI really offers, since each one you keep is a potential sort you must index.

findings.title: pgvector: choose HNSW, not IVFFlat, and plan for the filtered-search trap
findings.detail: Phase 5 is per-user similarity search over Fashion-CLIP embeddings, which is the worst case for IVFFlat: IVFFlat must be built on data that already exists and degrades as new rows diverge from its trained lists, whereas a wardrobe grows one garment at a time. Current guidance is that HNSW is the default for production — better speed/recall tradeoff, handles incremental inserts, and "the safer default when your dataset is under ~1 million rows, data arrives incrementally, and you prioritize recall"; one benchmark puts HNSW at 2,300 QPS vs IVFFlat's 680 on 1M 768-dim vectors. pgvector-python gives you this in Django directly: a VectorExtension() migration operation, VectorField(dimensions=...), and HnswIndex(name=..., fields=["embedding"], m=16, ef_construction=64, opclasses=["vector_cosine_ops"]) in Meta.indexes, with ordering via CosineDistance in order_by and .alias(distance=...).filter(distance__lt=...) for thresholds. Use vector_cosine_ops for CLIP (its embeddings are normalised). The non-obvious trap: "Steal the Look" must filter to the requesting user's own garments, and an ANN index plus a selective WHERE is the classic pre/post-filtering problem — HNSW walks the global graph and can return fewer than k rows after your owner filter is applied. Also build the index against the direct (non-pooled) endpoint with maintenance_work_mem raised.
findings.actionable: Add pgvector to requirements, a VectorExtension() migration, and the embedding field on a vision-app model (not on GarmentItem itself — keep the wide hot table narrow). Declare HnswIndex with vector_cosine_ops. For owner-scoped search, either over-fetch (order_by distance, take 5-10x k, filter in Python) or enable pgvector 0.8+ iterative scan; measure recall either way and write the number into the thesis. Run the index-creating migration through the direct endpoint.

findings.title: Adopt a services/selectors layer — the upload view is already doing four jobs, and it is what makes the AI calls testable
findings.detail: GarmentImageUploadView.post currently does size validation, content-type validation, background removal, two Cloudinary uploads, colour naming, and response shaping in one method. The HackSoft styleguide — the de facto reference here, and explicitly "tested in production" — puts business logic in services (functions that write) and selectors (functions that read), and explicitly argues against logic in "APIs and Views, Serializers and Forms, Model save methods, custom managers/querysets, Signals" because it "fragments the business logic in multiple places, making it really hard to trace the data flow." Its conventions are cheap to adopt: keyword-only args, type annotations, <entity>_<action> naming (garment_create, garment_mark_worn), transaction.atomic in the service. The payoff is specific to your project rather than abstract: every external dependency you are about to add (rembg, Cloudinary, OpenWeather, fal.ai) becomes mockable at one named seam, which is the precondition for the testing strategy below. On fat-vs-thin: your models are currently well judged — cost_per_wear and days_since_worn are exactly the "properties for simple derived values from non-relational fields" the styleguide endorses — but location_path and full_path span relations and should move out, which is the same conclusion the N+1 finding reaches from the other direction.
findings.actionable: Create apps/<app>/services.py and selectors.py. Move the upload orchestration into apps/vision/services.py (e.g. garment_image_process) and have the view only validate input and call it. Move location_path/full_path composition out of the models into a selector. Keep get_queryset() thin and delegate filtering to selectors as the filters get more complex in Phase 4. Do not refactor the whole project at once — apply it to new Phase 3+ code and to the upload path.

findings.title: Tests: must run on Postgres, and assertNumQueries is the guard that keeps the N+1 fixes fixed
findings.detail: Two problems. First, settings.py falls back to SQLite when DATABASE_URL is empty, which means tests run on SQLite by default — and ArrayField `contains`, GinIndex, pg_trgm and pgvector do not exist there, so exactly the query paths most likely to break are the ones never exercised. Every filter in GarmentItemFilter that touches seasons/occasions is currently untestable in CI. Second, nothing prevents the N+1s above from coming back the next time someone adds a field to a serializer. The standard stack is pytest-django + factory_boy for fixtures rather than raw Model.objects.create, DRF's APIClient/APITestCase for endpoints, --reuse-db and pytest-xdist for speed, and unittest.mock at the service boundary for third-party APIs. The piece most reviews omit and that matters most here is assertNumQueries: an explicit query-count assertion on each list endpoint turns an invisible performance regression into a red test. django-zen-queries is the stronger version — wrap serialization in queries_disabled() so any lazy load raises instead of quietly costing a query.
findings.actionable: Add a config/settings test path (or pytest.ini DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE) that requires a real Postgres DATABASE_URL and refuses to fall back to SQLite — run a local Postgres with pgvector in CI rather than testing against Neon. Add requirements/dev.txt: pytest-django, pytest-cov, factory-boy, django-zen-queries (plus django-debug-toolbar for local inspection). Write assertNumQueries tests for /api/wardrobe/items/, /locations/, /locations/tree/ and /items/?location=N. Structure tests per the styleguide: apps/<app>/tests/{factories.py,services/,selectors/,apis/}. Mock rembg/Cloudinary/fal.ai/OpenWeather at the service function, not at the HTTP library.

findings.title: No throttling in front of paid AI calls, and the cache backend choice decides whether throttling works at all
findings.detail: REST_FRAMEWORK configures no DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES. Today that is merely untidy; from Phase 3 it is a billing exposure, because OpenWeather, fal.ai try-on and Fashion-CLIP embedding are all metered per call and any authenticated user can loop them. DRF's ScopedRateThrottle is the right tool — views declare a throttle_scope and rates live in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES. Two caveats from the docs that change the implementation: throttling "should not be considered a security measure" (it is cost control, not abuse prevention), and it is built on Django's cache with non-atomic operations, so there is "some fuzziness" under concurrency. The practical consequence nobody mentions: with the default LocMemCache, each gunicorn worker keeps its own counters, so a "10/hour" limit silently becomes 10-per-hour-per-worker. A shared cache backend is a prerequisite, not an optimisation.
findings.actionable: Add DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES with UserRateThrottle + AnonRateThrottle and generous defaults, then set throttle_scope on each expensive endpoint (e.g. tryon: "5/hour", upload: "60/hour", weather: "30/hour") with matching DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES. Configure a shared CACHES backend — the database cache backend is enough here and avoids adding Redis. Cache OpenWeather responses per (city, hour) in the same cache; it is the single biggest reduction in external calls for the least work.

findings.title: Three small correctness bugs worth fixing while you are in these files
findings.detail: (1) GarmentItem.mark_worn does `self.wear_count += 1` then save(update_fields=...). That is a read-modify-write in Python: two concurrent mark-worn requests both read the same value and one increment is lost. Since wear_count is deliberately denormalised and feeds cost_per_wear, a lost update is a visibly wrong number in the thesis demo. Use an F() expression so the increment happens in the database. (2) bulk_move uses .update(storage_location=...), which bypasses save() and therefore does not fire auto_now on updated_at — moved items keep a stale timestamp, which will matter if you ever sync or cache on updated_at. Pass updated_at=timezone.now() explicitly in the update. (3) GarmentItem.__str__ returns f"{self.name} ({self.owner.email})", which dereferences owner — one extra query per object in the admin changelist and in any DRF error message that repr's a queryset. Also worth noting: SECRET_KEY has a default of "dev-only-insecure-key-change-me" and DATABASE_URL silently falls back to SQLite with only a print(), so a misconfigured production deploy boots successfully with a known signing key and an empty database instead of failing loudly.
findings.actionable: In models.py: mark_worn -> GarmentItem.objects.filter(pk=self.pk).update(wear_count=F("wear_count")+1, last_worn_date=..., updated_at=timezone.now()) then refresh_from_db, or use F() on the instance. Drop owner.email from __str__ (use owner_id if you need it) and add list_select_related = ("owner", "category") in admin.py. Add updated_at to the bulk_move update. In settings.py: make SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL required (env("SECRET_KEY") with no default) when DEBUG is False, and raise ImproperlyConfigured instead of print()-ing the SQLite fallback.

summary:

Three confirmed live defects in the current code, all of which will bite later:
(1) D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\api.ts sets `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }` on the axios instance. Confirmed in the installed axios 1.20.0 source that this makes any FormData POST get silently JSON-stringified instead of uploaded — file uploads will send `{}` instead of the file. (2) D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\globals.css compiles to `:root { --font-sans: var(--font-sans) }` (verified in the emitted CSS at .next/dev/static/chunks/src_app_globals_css_*.css line 93) because next/font's `variable: "--font-sans"` collides with the Tailwind `@theme inline` token of the same name. Self-referential custom property = invalid at computed-value time; whether Outfit renders at all depends on stylesheet source order.
(3) D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\tabs.tsx destructures `orientation` out of props and never forwards it to `Tabs.Root`, so `<Tabs orientation="vertical">` styles vertically but keeps horizontal arrow-key navigation.

Also: the "base-nova" registry is overwriting hand-edits (input.tsx changed on disk mid-session), Base UI's API differs from Radix in more places than asChild→render (Group/GroupLabel nesting, Select.Label vs Select.GroupLabel, Tabs.Tab/Panel, Positioner vs Content, data-open vs data-state), and globals.css's three @import lines are all load-bearing — `@import "shadcn/tailwind.css"` is what defines the `data-open:` / `data-closed:` / `data-checked:` variants every generated component uses.

Findings below are ordered: Base UI API (1-12), Next.js 16 (13-19), Tailwind v4 (20-24), TanStack Query v5 (25-29), axios + upload (30-33), accessibility (34-36).

findings.title: BASE UI 1: `render` replaces `asChild`, and the passed element must forward ref + spread props
findings.detail: Radix's `asChild` + Slot is gone. Base UI parts take `render`, which accepts either a ReactElement or a function `(props, state) => ReactElement`. The element you hand to `render` is responsible for forwarding its ref and spreading every received prop onto its DOM node — Base UI does not wrap it in a Slot that does this for you. Nesting composition is done by nesting `render` props (Tooltip.Trigger render={} />}), not by stacking asChild. The function form also gives you the part's state, which is how you render different content per state (e.g. `(props, state) => {state.checked ? : }`). The existing code already uses this correctly in dialog.tsx (`}>`) and select.tsx (`} />`) — follow that shape.
findings.actionable: Never write `asChild` in this project. When you need a Base UI part to render one of your own components, pass `render={<YourComponent />}` and put children on the Base UI part, not inside the render element. Any custom component used in `render` must be `function X({...props}) { return <el {...props} /> }` — no dropped props, no swallowed ref. Grep for `asChild` before committing: `grep -rn asChild D:\FYP\frontend\src`.

findings.title: BASE UI 2: positioning props belong on `Positioner`, never on `Popup` — popups are a 4-part chain
findings.detail: Radix put `side`/`align`/`sideOffset` on `*Content`. Base UI splits that content into `Portal > Backdrop > Positioner > Popup`. `Positioner` owns placement; `Popup` owns the box. The generated wrappers in this project encode this correctly by typing the public prop bag as `Popup.Props & Pick<Positioner.Props, "align"|"alignOffset"|"side"|"sideOffset">` and splitting them internally (see SelectContent and DropdownMenuContent). Full anatomies: Select = Root/Label/Trigger(Value,Icon)/Portal/Backdrop/Positioner/Popup/ScrollUpArrow/Arrow/List(Item(ItemText,ItemIndicator),Separator,Group(GroupLabel))/ScrollDownArrow. Dialog = Root/Trigger/Portal/Backdrop/Viewport/Popup(Title,Description,Close). Popover = Root/Trigger/Portal/Backdrop/Positioner/Popup(Arrow,Viewport(Title,Description,Close)). Menu = Root/Trigger/Portal/Backdrop/Positioner/Popup(Arrow,Item,LinkItem,Separator,SubmenuRoot(SubmenuTrigger),Group(GroupLabel),RadioGroup(GroupLabel,RadioItem(RadioItemIndicator)),CheckboxItem(CheckboxItemIndicator),Viewport).
findings.actionable: When adding Popover/Tooltip/Combobox/AlertDialog wrappers, copy the split-props pattern already used in D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\select.tsx and dropdown-menu.tsx. Do NOT put `side`/`align`/`sideOffset` on a `*.Popup`. Base UI has no `*.Content` part at all — if you type `SomethingPrimitive.Content`, it does not exist.

findings.title: BASE UI 3: `GroupLabel` only works inside `Group` — a loose label has no accessible association
findings.detail: Base UI docs describe GroupLabel as "An accessible label that is automatically associated with its parent group." The association is implicit via the parent `Group` (or `Menu.RadioGroup`). In Radix you could drop `<SelectLabel>` anywhere inside the content; here, a `GroupLabel` outside a `Group` renders a bare `<div>` with no `aria-labelledby` wiring, so screen readers announce a stray text node and the items get no section name.
findings.actionable: Always write `<SelectGroup><SelectLabel>Tops</SelectLabel><SelectItem .../></SelectGroup>` and `<DropdownMenuGroup><DropdownMenuLabel>…</DropdownMenuLabel>…</DropdownMenuGroup>`. For the Select grouped-data shape, Base UI expects `items` as an array of `{ value: <heading>, items: [...] }` objects when you use `Select.Root items={groups}`.

findings.title: BASE UI 4: `Select.Label` ≠ `Select.GroupLabel` — this project's `SelectLabel` is the group one, so every Select currently has no accessible name
findings.detail: Base UI has two distinct parts: `Select.Label` ("automatically associated with the select trigger", renders a `<div>` so clicking it focuses the trigger without opening the popup) and `Select.GroupLabel` (section heading inside the popup). D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\select.tsx exports `SelectLabel` mapped to `SelectPrimitive.GroupLabel` and does NOT export a wrapper for `Select.Label`. Base UI's own usage guideline is explicit: "Form controls must have an accessible name: Prefer `<Select.Label>`, or provide an `aria-label` on `<Select.Trigger>` when no visible label is rendered." A `<Label htmlFor>` from label.tsx will not work here either — the trigger is a `<button>`, and Base UI's Select has no labelable input exposed for `htmlFor`.
findings.actionable: Either (a) add a `SelectFieldLabel` export wrapping `SelectPrimitive.Label` to D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\select.tsx and use it inside `<Select>` above the trigger, or (b) put `aria-label="Category"` on every `<SelectTrigger>`. Do (a) wherever a visible label exists. Do not pair a plain `<Label htmlFor>` with `<SelectTrigger>` and assume it's wired.

findings.title: BASE UI 5: `Select.Value` renders the RAW value unless you pass `items` to `Select.Root`
findings.detail: In Radix, `<SelectValue/>` picked up the selected item's text children automatically. In Base UI it renders the raw `value` by default, so a select of `{value:'tshirt', label:'T-shirt'}` shows "tshirt" in the trigger. Three documented fixes: pass `items` to `Select.Root` (array of `{label, value}`, or a `Record<string, ReactNode>` lookup map, or grouped objects) and the matching label is rendered; or pass a children function `<Select.Value>{(v) => …}</Select.Value>`; or use object values per item plus `itemToStringLabel`. Related: with object item values, `isItemEqualToValue` is needed because comparison defaults to `Object.is`, and `itemToStringValue` controls what the hidden input submits. Placeholder text goes on `Select.Value` via `placeholder="…"`, and once a placeholder is used the user can no longer clear the value from the popup unless you render an explicit `{ value: null, label: '…' }` item.
findings.actionable: Define category/season/colour option arrays once (e.g. in D:\FYP\frontend\src\types\wardrobe.ts) as `{label, value}[]`, then always `<Select items={OPTIONS} value={…} onValueChange={…}>` plus `<SelectValue placeholder="Choose a category" />`. For any select whose values are objects (outfit items, storage locations), also pass `isItemEqualToValue={(a,b)=>a.id===b.id}`.

findings.title: BASE UI 6: Select's `alignItemWithTrigger` defaults to true and IGNORES side/align — and the wrapper hard-codes it on
findings.detail: Base UI's Select positioner overlaps the trigger by default so the selected item's text lines up with the trigger's value text. The docs state: "Other positioning props are ignored: Props like `side` or `align` have no effect unless the prop is set to `false` or when in fallback mode." It also auto-disables on touch, and falls back when there's not enough viewport room (trigger must be ≥20px from the top/bottom edges; tune via `min-height` on the Positioner). In that mode `data-side="none"` is set on Popup and Positioner. D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\select.tsx defaults `alignItemWithTrigger = true` and `side="bottom"`/`align="center"` — so the side/align defaults there are dead props most of the time, and the popup will appear to "jump" position between desktop mouse, touch, and near-viewport-edge cases.

Expect and style the `data-[side=none]` case (the wrapper already has `data-[align-trigger=true]:animate-none`). If a Select needs deterministic dropdown-below-trigger behaviour (filter bars, toolbars), set `alignItemWithTrigger={false}` explicitly at the call site.

findings.title: BASE UI 7: every change handler is `(value, eventDetails)` — use `eventDetails.reason` / `.cancel()` instead of controlling state just to veto a change
findings.detail: Base UI's `onOpenChange`, `onValueChange`, `onCheckedChange`, `onPressedChange` all receive a second `eventDetails` argument: `{ reason, event, cancel(), allowPropagation(), isCanceled, isPropagationAllowed, trigger }`. `cancel()` blocks the component's internal state change, which means you can keep a component uncontrolled and still veto specific transitions — the documented alternative to hoisting state. `reason` is a typed union (for Select: 'trigger-press' | 'outside-press' | 'escape-key' | 'window-resize' | 'item-press' | 'focus-out' | 'list-navigation' | 'cancel-open' | 'none'). Esc normally stops propagation so nested popups don't all close; `allowPropagation()` opts out.
findings.actionable: For the "unsaved changes" confirm on an item-edit Dialog, use `onOpenChange={(open, d) => { if (!open && isDirty && d.reason !== 'none') { d.cancel(); setConfirmOpen(true) } }}` rather than a controlled `open` + guard. Also note `onOpenChange={setOpen}` is still safe (the 2nd arg is ignored by setState), but `onValueChange={field.onChange}` from react-hook-form passes eventDetails as RHF's 2nd arg — prefer `onValueChange={(v) => field.onChange(v)}`.

findings.title: BASE UI 8: Tabs uses `Tab`/`Panel` (not Trigger/Content), `Panel.value` is REQUIRED, and `defaultValue` is index-based `0`
findings.detail: Base UI Tabs anatomy is `Tabs.Root > Tabs.List > Tabs.Tab + Tabs.Indicator`, plus `Tabs.Panel`. `Panel` has `value` marked required (`value*`) and a `keepMounted` prop (default false — panel content unmounts when hidden). `Tabs.Root.defaultValue` defaults to `0`, i.e. tabs are index-addressed when you omit values, unlike Radix which required matching string values. `onValueChange` carries a reason union ('none' for user clicks, plus 'initial' | 'disabled' | 'missing' for automatic fallbacks that cannot be cancelled).
findings.actionable: Always give both `<TabsTrigger value="x">` and `<TabsContent value="x">` the same explicit string value — never rely on the index default, because inserting a tab silently reassigns selection. If a tab panel hosts an uncontrolled form or a mounted chart you don't want torn down, pass `keepMounted`. Treat `reason !== 'none'` in `onValueChange` as a programmatic fallback, not a user action (don't fire analytics/navigation on it).

findings.title: BASE UI 10: Checkbox takes a boolean `indeterminate` prop — not Radix's `checked="indeterminate"`
findings.detail: Base UI `Checkbox.Root` renders "a `<span>` element and a hidden `<input>` beside" it. Props: `checked` (boolean|undefined), `defaultChecked`, `onCheckedChange(checked: boolean, eventDetails)`, and a separate `indeterminate: boolean`. There is no `"indeterminate"` value for `checked`, so Radix-era code that does `checked={allSelected ? true : someSelected ? 'indeterminate' : false}` is a type error and a logic error. Other notable props: `value` (falls back to `name`), `uncheckedValue` (by default unchecked boxes submit nothing, matching native), `parent` (for CheckboxGroup tri-state), `inputRef`, and `nativeButton` which defaults to **false** here (the inverse of Trigger parts, which default to true) — set it true only if your `render` element is a real `<button>`.

When filtering by multiple tags, prefer `CheckboxGroup` + `Field.Item` over hand-rolled arrays. If you ever pass `render={<button/>}` to Checkbox, add `nativeButton`.

findings.title: BASE UI 11: Dialog — `Backdrop` not `Overlay`, `Popup` not `Content`, `Close` must live inside `Popup` when modal, `Viewport` is a real part
findings.detail: Base UI Dialog: `modal` defaults to `true` and accepts `true | false | 'trap-focus'`. The docs add a hard requirement: "When `modal` is `true` or `'trap-focus'`, render `<Dialog.Close>` inside `<Dialog.Popup>` so touch screen readers can escape the popup" (Popover goes further: with `modal={true}`, focus trapping is only enabled if a `Popover.Close` is inside the Popup — it may be `sr-only`). Focus is configured with `initialFocus`/`finalFocus` on **Popup** (boolean | RefObject | `(interactionType) => …`); by default focus goes to the first tabbable element, except on touch where the popup itself is focused to avoid popping the virtual keyboard. Other Root props worth knowing: `disablePointerDismissal` (replaces Radix's onPointerDownOutside preventDefault dance), `actionsRef` ({unmount, close}), `handle`/`triggerId` for detached and multiple triggers, and `onOpenChangeComplete` for after-animation work. Popup exposes `data-nested`, `data-nested-dialog-open` and `--nested-dialogs` for stacked dialogs. The anatomy also includes `Dialog.Viewport` (between Backdrop and Popup) which this project's wrapper omits — fine for centred dialogs, needed for inside-scroll/outside-scroll layouts.
findings.actionable: Keep `showCloseButton` on by default in D:\FYP\frontend\src\components\ui\dialog.tsx — turning it off on a modal dialog breaks touch screen-reader escape. For the "add item" form dialog, set `initialFocus` to the first text input's ref so focus doesn't land on a file-picker button. Use `disablePointerDismissal` (not an onOpenChange guard) to stop accidental outside-click dismissal during an upload. If you build a tall scrolling dialog, add `DialogPrimitive.Viewport` rather than making the Popup itself scroll.

findings.title: BASE UI 12: animation attributes are `data-starting-style`/`data-ending-style` for transitions and `data-open`/`data-closed` for keyframes — and `@import "shadcn/tailwind.css"` is what makes `data-open:` compile
findings.detail: Base UI's animation contract: `[data-starting-style]`/`[data-ending-style]` are the transition endpoints (recommended, because transitions cancel smoothly mid-flight), while `[data-open]`/`[data-closed]` are for CSS keyframe animations. There is no `data-state="open"` like Radix. The generated components in this project use Tailwind variants `data-open:animate-in`, `data-closed:animate-out`, `data-checked:bg-primary` — those variants are not built into Tailwind v4; they are defined in D:\FYP\frontend\node_modules\shadcn\tailwind.css as `@custom-variant data-open { &:where([data-state="open"]), &:where([data-open]:not([data-open="false"])) { @slot } }` (same for data-closed/data-checked/data-unchecked/data-selected), and `animate-in`/`fade-in-0`/`zoom-in-95`/`slide-in-from-top-2` come from `tw-animate-css`. So all three `@import` lines at the top of globals.css are load-bearing. For JS animation (Motion), the documented recipe is: control `open`, put `keepMounted` on the `Portal`, compose the Popup via `render={<motion.div/>}`, and always animate opacity (even to 0.9999) because Base UI uses `element.getAnimations()` to decide when it may unmount.
findings.actionable: Do not remove or reorder the three imports in D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\globals.css (`tailwindcss`, `tw-animate-css`, `shadcn/tailwind.css`) — dropping the third makes every `data-open:`/`data-checked:` class silently no-op with no build error. For new hand-written popup styling prefer the transition form (`transition-[scale,opacity] data-starting-style:opacity-0 data-ending-style:opacity-0`) over keyframes. If you add Motion later, follow the keepMounted + render recipe, not AnimatePresence alone.

findings.title: BASE UI 13: forms — Base UI's own `Field`/`Form` has a documented react-hook-form integration; the current pages use neither
findings.detail: Base UI ships `Field` (Root/Label/Control/Description/Item/Error/Validity) and `Form`, and documents the exact RHF bridge: wrap in `<Controller>` and map `fieldState` onto `Field.Root` — `<Field.Root name={name} invalid={invalid} touched={isTouched} dirty={isDirty}>`, then `<Field.Control value={value} onBlur={onBlur} onValueChange={onChange} ref={ref} />`, then `<Field.Error match={!!error}>{error?.message}</Field.Error>`. Note `onValueChange` (value-first) rather than `onChange`, and the warning that RHF can only focus invalid fields if your wrapper forwards the ref — "typically accomplish this using the `inputRef` prop". Labeling rules by control type: `Field.Label` or native `<label>` for Input/NumberField/OTPField/Autocomplete/Checkbox/Radio/Switch (Checkbox/Radio/Switch may be implicitly labelled by nesting inside `Field.Label`); `Select.Label` for Select; `Combobox.Label` for Combobox-with-input-in-popup; `Fieldset.Root` + `Fieldset.Legend` + one `Field.Item` per option for checkbox/radio groups; `aria-label` only as the fallback when nothing visible exists. Meanwhile D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\(auth)\login\page.tsx uses raw `useState` per field even though react-hook-form 7.87, @hookform/resolvers 5.9 and zod 4.5 are all installed and unused, and D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\api.ts already exposes `getFieldErrors()` that nothing consumes.
findings.actionable: Pick ONE forms approach now and apply it everywhere: either (a) adopt `Field` + `Controller` exactly as documented (best a11y — you get automatic label/description/error association for free), or (b) stay with plain `<Label htmlFor>` + `<Input id>` + RHF `register()` and wire `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` by hand. Given react-hook-form + zod + getFieldErrors() are already installed, rewrite login/register with `useForm({resolver: zodResolver(schema)})` and feed `getFieldErrors(error)` into `setError()` on a 400 response. Base UI Input's `onValueChange` is invisible to TS because input.tsx types props as `React.ComponentProps<"input">` — widen it to `InputPrimitive.Props` if you want it.

findings.title: NEXT 16: reading localStorage during render causes hydration errors — `suppressHydrationWarning` is per-element and lets the DOM win
findings.detail: Next's dedicated guide spells out the three bad options (client re-render → hydration error; useEffect → visible flash; server-only → no client values) and the one good one: an inline `<script>` via dangerouslySetInnerHTML that runs synchronously during HTML parsing, before first paint, on an element carrying `suppressHydrationWarning`. Two caveats that matter: without the attribute, React recovers by client-rendering from the nearest error/Suspense boundary, and "inline script corrections on **other components within that boundary are lost**"; with it, "React keeps whatever is in the DOM and discards the client's output for that element" — so it suppresses real bugs too, and it does not cascade deeply. Also relevant: scripts inserted by DOM updates don't run on soft navigations, so the component must be a Client Component for client-side nav to work. Relevant here: `tokens.isLoggedIn()` is read during render in `useCurrentUser()`'s `enabled` option (src\hooks\use-auth.ts), and `next-themes` needs `suppressHydrationWarning` on `<html>` (already present in src\app\layout.tsx — keep it).
findings.actionable: Never read localStorage, `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `window.*` or `toLocaleDateString()` in the render body of a component that SSRs. For dates across the app (item added-on, planner days) build the documented `LocalDate` + `InlineScript` pair rather than formatting in a client component. When debugging with `TZ=UTC LANG=ja_JP.UTF-8 next dev`, locale mismatches surface immediately. Do not sprinkle `suppressHydrationWarning` to silence warnings — on `<html>` for next-themes only.

findings.title: NEXT 16: `images.domains` is deprecated → `remotePatterns`; plus middleware→proxy, parallel-route `default.js`, scroll-behavior, revalidateTag arity
findings.detail: A grab-bag of Next 16 breaking changes that this project will hit as it grows. (a) `images.domains` deprecated in favour of `images.remotePatterns: [{protocol, hostname, port, pathname}]` — required before any `next/image` can render Django MEDIA_URL uploads. Also in 16: local images with query strings are a breaking change, `minimumCacheTTL`/`imageSizes`/`qualities` defaults changed, local IP hosts are restricted, and `next/legacy/image` is deprecated. (b) `middleware.ts` → `proxy.ts` with the named export renamed `middleware` → `proxy`; proxy is nodejs-runtime-only and not configurable (stay on `middleware` if you need edge); config flags renamed, e.g. `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize` → `skipProxyUrlNormalize`. (c) "All parallel route slots now require explicit `default.js` files. Builds will fail without them" — relevant if you add an `@modal` intercepted-route for the item detail view. (d) Next no longer overrides your global `scroll-behavior: smooth` on navigation; add `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` to `<html>` to restore instant scroll-to-top. (e) `revalidateTag('x')` now needs a cacheLife profile: `revalidateTag('x','max')`; `updateTag(tag)` is the Server-Actions-only read-your-writes version; PPR is now `cacheComponents: true` (the `experimental.ppr` flag and `experimental_ppr` segment export are removed, as are `experimental.dynamicIO`/`experimental.useCache`). ESLint defaults to flat config, and `next lint` is removed (this project is already on eslint.config.mjs + `"lint": "eslint"` — correct).
findings.actionable: Before the first wardrobe photo renders, add to D:\FYP\frontend\next.config.ts: `images: { remotePatterns: [{ protocol: 'http', hostname: 'localhost', port: '8000', pathname: '/media/**' }] }` and a production entry for the deployed Django host. If you ever add an auth-redirect at the edge, create `proxy.ts` with `export function proxy(request) {}`, not middleware.ts. If you add `@modal` parallel routes, ship `default.tsx` in every slot. Don't call `revalidateTag` with one argument.

findings.title: TAILWIND v4: the v3 defaults that silently changed — border/ring colour, ring width, `outline-none`
findings.detail: Default border colour went from `gray-200` to `currentColor`, and ring went from 3px/blue-500 to 1px/currentColor — so `border` alone now draws in the text colour, and bare `ring` is a hairline. `outline-none` now genuinely means `outline-style: none`; the old "invisible but present" behaviour is `outline-hidden`. This project is partially protected: globals.css has `@layer base { * { @apply border-border outline-ring/50 } }`, and the generated components already use `ring-3` and `outline-hidden` where they mean it. Hand-written markup is where the regressions appear.
findings.actionable: In new markup never rely on bare `border` or bare `ring` to carry a colour — write `border border-border`, and `ring-3 ring-ring/50` for focus rings. Use `outline-hidden` (not `outline-none`) when you're replacing the outline with a ring. Reuse the focus recipe the generated components already use: `focus-visible:border-ring focus-visible:ring-3 focus-visible:ring-ring/50`.
findings.source: https://tailwindcss.com/docs/upgrade-guide (Default border color; Default ring width and color; outline-none renamed)

findings.title: TAILWIND v4: syntax changes that fail silently — variant order, `!` position, `(--var)` arbitrary values, `space-y` selector
findings.detail: Variants now stack left-to-right like CSS (`*:first:pt-0`, not `first:*:pt-0`). The important modifier moved to the end (`flex!`, not `!flex`). Arbitrary values that reference a CSS variable use parentheses: `bg-(--brand)`, not `bg-[--brand]` — you can see the new form all over the generated components (`max-h-(--available-height)`, `w-(--anchor-width)`, `origin-(--transform-origin)`). `space-y-*`/`divide-*` changed from `> :not([hidden]) ~ :not([hidden])` to `> :not(:last-child)`, which changes behaviour with inline elements and with conditionally-rendered children; the docs recommend flex/grid + `gap`. `transition`/`transition-colors` now include `outline-color`, so focus outlines can animate unexpectedly unless the outline colour is set unconditionally. `hover:` is wrapped in `@media (hover: hover)` so it no longer sticks on touch. Renamed scales: `shadow-sm`→`shadow-xs`, `shadow`→`shadow-sm`, `rounded-sm`→`rounded-xs`, `blur-sm`→`blur-xs`.
findings.actionable: The existing pages use `space-y-4`/`space-y-2` (src\app\(auth)\login\page.tsx); convert those to `flex flex-col gap-4` as you touch them, and use gap for all new vertical rhythm. Write `bg-(--x)` and `flex!` forms. When copying any Tailwind snippet from a blog or from training memory, assume v3 syntax and check these five items.
findings.source: https://tailwindcss.com/docs/upgrade-guide (Variant stacking order; Important modifier; CSS variables in arbitrary values; Space-between selector; Transitioning outline-color; Hover styles on mobile; Renamed utilities)

findings.title: TAILWIND v4: `@theme inline` vs `@theme`, `@utility` not `@layer utilities`, `@reference` for `@apply` in other files, no JS config autodiscovery
findings.detail: Custom utilities must use `@utility name { … }`; `@layer utilities { .x {} }` no longer produces a real utility (no variant support). There is no auto-detected tailwind.config.js — it must be loaded explicitly with `@config "…"`, and `corePlugins`, `safelist` and `separator` aren't supported at all (this project correctly has `"config": ""` in components.json and no JS config). The `theme()` function is discouraged in favour of `var(--color-…)`, and in media queries it takes variable names: `@media (width >= theme(--breakpoint-xl))`. `@apply` inside a separate stylesheet (CSS module, Vue/Svelte block) can't see the theme and needs `@reference "../../app.css"` first. `@theme inline` (used throughout this project's globals.css) resolves the token into the utility instead of emitting a `var()` indirection — which is exactly why the `--font-sans: var(--font-sans)` self-reference above is so easy to write by accident. Keep `@tailwindcss/postcss` first in the PostCSS plugin list (correct in D:\FYP\frontend\postcss.config.mjs).
findings.actionable: Add shared design utilities with `@utility` in globals.css, never `@layer utilities`. Don't introduce a tailwind.config.js. When adding a theme token, give it a name distinct from anything defined outside the `@theme` block (the font bug is the cautionary tale), and add both the `:root` and `.dark` values at the same time. If you add CSS modules, put `@reference` at the top.

findings.title: TAILWIND v4 + shadcn: `cn` replaces clsx+tailwind-merge, components import it from `"cn"` (bypassing `@/lib/utils`), and custom theme keys need `cn/config`
findings.detail: This project has no `tailwind-merge` installed; `cn` 0.2.6 ("Fast, small, compiled class-name merging… Drop-in replacement for clsx + tailwind-merge", by aidenybai + shadcn) is the engine, and D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\utils.ts is just `export { cn } from "cn"`. Every generated component imports `from "cn"` directly, so the `"utils": "@/lib/utils"` alias in components.json is effectively bypassed — editing lib/utils.ts will not change component behaviour. Like tailwind-merge, `cn` needs to be told about custom class groups to resolve conflicts correctly; it exposes `cn/config` accepting the same `{ extend, override, prefix }` shape as `extendTailwindMerge`. This project adds non-default theme keys (`--color-success`, `--color-warning`, `--radius-4xl`, `--font-heading`, the whole sidebar scale), so conflict resolution between e.g. `bg-success` and `bg-primary` is worth verifying.
findings.actionable: Don't try to customise `cn` by editing src\lib\utils.ts — create a `cn/config` setup if you need custom class groups. Sanity-check one case in a scratch test: `cn("bg-primary", "bg-success")` must yield `"bg-success"`. Also note components import from `"cn"`, so if you later want a wrapped/instrumented cn you must alias the bare `"cn"` specifier, not the alias.

findings.title: TAILWIND v4: the dark variant `&:is(.dark *)` excludes `<html class="dark">` itself
findings.detail: D:\FYP\frontend\src\app\globals.css declares `@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));`. `next-themes` with `attribute="class"` puts `class="dark"` on `<html>`, and `.dark *` matches only *descendants* of `.dark` — so a `dark:` utility applied to `<html>` itself never fires. Everything inside `<body>` works, so this is latent rather than broken today, but it bites the moment you put a `dark:` class on the html element or build a component that can be the root. The more robust form shadcn now uses is `&:where(.dark, .dark *)`, which matches the toggled element and its subtree and keeps zero specificity.

Also note `ThemeProvider` is currently `defaultTheme="light" enableSystem={false}` in src\providers\app-providers.tsx, so the dark palette in globals.css is unreachable from the UI — either wire a theme toggle or drop the claim that dark mode is supported.

findings.title: QUERY v5: mutation callback argument order changed — the 3rd arg is `onMutateResult`, the LAST arg is the new `context`
findings.detail:
Verified against the installed types in D:\FYP\frontend\node_modules\@tanstack\query-core\build\modern\hydration-Bjs0MSgg.d.ts (lines 1178-1190):

  type MutationFunctionContext = { client: QueryClient; meta: MutationMeta | undefined; mutationKey?: MutationKey }
  onMutate?: (variables, context: MutationFunctionContext) => Promise<TOnMutateResult> | TOnMutateResult
  onSuccess?: (data, variables, onMutateResult, context) => …
  onError?:   (error, variables, onMutateResult, context) => …
  onSettled?: (data, error, variables, onMutateResult, context) => …

Older v5 tutorials call the 3rd argument "context" (it was the onMutate return value). In 5.102 that slot is named `onMutateResult` and a genuinely new `context` — carrying `client`, `meta`, `mutationKey` — is appended last. `mutationFn` itself also receives `(variables, context)`. Positionally the old rollback code still works, which is exactly why the naming trap is dangerous: `onError: (e, v, context) => setQueryData(key, context.previous)` compiles and works, but the name now lies, and anyone adding a 4th parameter will reach for the wrong thing.
findings.actionable: Name the parameters honestly in every mutation in this project: `onError: (error, variables, rollback) => { if (rollback) queryClient.setQueryData(key, rollback.previous) }`. Prefer `context.client` inside `onMutate`/`mutationFn` over closing over `useQueryClient()` when you want the mutation options to be reusable outside a component. Do not copy a v4-era `onMutate(variables)`-only signature.

findings.title: QUERY v5: the two optimistic-update patterns — pick by how many places show the change
findings.detail: Pattern A (preferred when one spot renders the pending item): don't touch the cache at all. Read `variables`, `isPending` and `isError` off the mutation and render a translucent pending row, with `onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey })` and a retry button wired to `mutate(variables)`. Pattern B (when several components must reflect the change): `onMutate: async (vars, ctx) => { await ctx.client.cancelQueries({queryKey}); const previous = ctx.client.getQueryData(queryKey); ctx.client.setQueryData(queryKey, old => …); return { previous } }`, `onError: (e, v, rollback) => queryClient.setQueryData(queryKey, rollback?.previous)`, `onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({queryKey})`. The `cancelQueries` step is not optional — without it an in-flight refetch can land after your optimistic write and clobber it. Caveat from the docs: with several concurrent mutations, `useMutationState` returns an array and you need something like `submittedAt` to tell them apart.
findings.actionable: Use Pattern A for wardrobe-item creation (the new card only appears in one list). Use Pattern B for favourite/worn-count toggles and outfit planner assignment, where the same item renders in a grid, a detail panel and a counter. Always include all three callbacks — an optimistic write with no `onError` rollback is how the UI ends up lying about server state. Keep the existing correct habit from src\hooks\use-auth.ts of `setQueryData(ME_QUERY_KEY, data)` after a profile PATCH instead of invalidating.
findings.source: https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/optimistic-updates; D:\FYP\frontend\node_modules\next\dist\docs\01-app\02-guides\client-side-data-fetching\tanstack-query.md (## Coordinate server and client caches after mutations)

findings.title: QUERY v5: infinite lists — `initialPageParam` is required and `getNextPageParam` takes four arguments
findings.detail: From the installed types: `getNextPageParam: (lastPage, allPages, lastPageParam, allPageParams) => TPageParam | undefined | null` is **required**, and `initialPageParam: TPageParam` is required (v4's `pageParam` defaulting is gone). Returning `undefined` or `null` is what sets `hasNextPage` false. `data` is `{ pages: TData[], pageParams: TPageParam[] }`, so you render `data.pages.flatMap(p => p.results)`. `maxPages` caps how many pages stay in memory. Two documented caveats: when an infinite query goes stale, "each group is fetched sequentially, starting from the first one" (so a stale 10-page wardrobe list is 10 sequential requests — another reason to keep `staleTime` meaningful), and "a single cache entry is shared for all pages, attempting to fetch twice simultaneously might lead to data overwrites" — so guard `fetchNextPage` with `!isFetchingNextPage`.
findings.actionable: For the wardrobe grid with Django REST pagination, use `initialPageParam: 1` with `getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next ? lastPage.page + 1 : undefined` (or parse `next`/`cursor` straight from the DRF response). Drive the sentinel with `onIntersect: () => { if (hasNextPage && !isFetchingNextPage) fetchNextPage() }`. Use `isFetchingNextPage` for the bottom spinner and `isFetching` for the top refresh hint — they are different states.

findings.title: QUERY v5: query keys — hierarchical factories + `queryOptions()`, so `invalidateQueries` prefix-matching does the work
findings.detail: Keys should run generic → specific so prefix matching gives you free invalidation granularity: `['wardrobe']` / `['wardrobe','list']` / `['wardrobe','list',{filters}]` / `['wardrobe','detail',id]`. Build them with a per-feature factory that composes on itself (`lists: () => [...keys.all,'list'] as const`), colocated with the feature rather than in a global utils file, and always arrays even for a single segment. Pair the key with its fetcher using `queryOptions({queryKey, queryFn, staleTime})` so a prefetch on the server and a `useQuery`/`useSuspenseQuery` on the client provably share one identity — Next's own guide stresses "The server and Client Component must use the same query key. Keep the key and query options together so both call sites share the same identity." This project currently has exactly one key (`ME_QUERY_KEY = ['auth','me'] as const` in src\hooks\use-auth.ts) and no factories.
findings.actionable: Before writing the wardrobe/outfits/planner hooks, create a `queryOptions`-based contract per feature, e.g. src\lib\queries\wardrobe.ts exporting `wardrobeKeys` plus `wardrobeQueries.list(filters)` / `.detail(id)`. Then `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: wardrobeKeys.lists() })` after a create, and `setQueryData(wardrobeKeys.detail(id), …)` after an edit. Never inline a raw string-array key at a call site. Use `refetchType: 'none'` when you want to mark stale without refetching offscreen lists.

findings.title: QUERY v5: `enabled: tokens.isLoggedIn()` reads localStorage during render — non-reactive and server/client divergent
findings.detail: D:\FYP\frontend\src\hooks\use-auth.ts does `enabled: tokens.isLoggedIn()` inside `useCurrentUser()`. `tokens.isLoggedIn()` returns `null`→false on the server and possibly true in the browser, so the query's enabled state differs between the SSR pass and hydration, and it is not reactive to login/logout within a mounted tree (it only re-evaluates when the component happens to re-render). Today this is masked because src\app\(app)\layout.tsx gates rendering behind a `checked` state that starts false in both environments, so the markup matches — but the masking is accidental and will break when a non-gated component calls `useCurrentUser()`. Per the Next guide, `enabled` is the right tool for deferring a request until an input exists; the problem is the *source* of the boolean.
findings.actionable: Make token presence a reactive, SSR-safe value: expose `useHasToken()` built on `useSyncExternalStore` (getSnapshot reads localStorage, getServerSnapshot returns false, subscribe listens to `storage` plus a local event dispatched by tokens.save/clear), then `enabled: hasToken`. Have tokens.save()/clear() dispatch that event so login/logout propagate without a reload. Keep `retry: false` on /auth/me/ — a 401 there genuinely means not-logged-in.

findings.title: QUERY v5 + NEXT 16: QueryClient creation, and `dehydrate()` is unsafe under Cache Components
findings.detail: Next's own TanStack guide recommends the browser-singleton shape — `if (typeof window === 'undefined') return new QueryClient(); browserQueryClient ??= new QueryClient(); return browserQueryClient` — which survives a Suspense-triggered re-render of the provider; this project uses `useState(() => new QueryClient(...))` in src\providers\app-providers.tsx, which is TanStack's other sanctioned pattern and is fine for a client-only data app. Two forward-looking traps if you ever turn on `cacheComponents`: Next then prerenders Client Components, and both `dehydrate()` and active-query creation read `Date.now()`, which raises a current-time prerender error — the documented fixes are to keep such queries behind `<Suspense>` and to hand-build the dehydrated state from a `'use cache'`-wrapped timestamp tagged with the same cacheTags as the data. Server-provided initial data also needs a real `staleTime` (the guide uses 30_000) or the client refetches immediately on hydration. Separately, `@tanstack/react-query-devtools` is installed but never rendered.
findings.actionable: Keep the `useState` QueryClient unless you add server prefetching; if you do, switch to the singleton shape from the Next guide and always pair `prefetchQuery` + `HydrationBoundary` with a non-zero `staleTime` on the shared `queryOptions`. Do not enable `cacheComponents` in next.config.ts without reading that guide's prerenderable-hydration section first. Render `<ReactQueryDevtools initialIsOpen={false} />` inside AppProviders guarded by `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'` so the installed dep earns its place. Also reconsider the global `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` — for weather-driven outfit suggestions, refetch-on-focus is the feature, so set it per-query rather than off everywhere.

findings.title: AXIOS (CRITICAL BUG): the instance's `Content-Type: application/json` will silently turn every FormData upload into JSON
findings.actionable: Delete the `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }` line from the `axios.create()` call in D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\api.ts and let axios infer it. If you must keep it for some reason, every multipart call needs `api.post(url, formData, { headers: { 'Content-Type': undefined } })`. findings.title: AXIOS: never set `multipart/form-data` yourself — and upload progress only works on the XHR adapter
findings.detail: The companion rule to the above: do not "fix" the problem by setting `Content-Type: multipart/form-data`, because then the boundary is missing and the server rejects the body ("Multipart: Boundary not found"). The browser/runtime generates the boundary when you leave the header alone. Axios itself defends against this in the fetch adapter — it deletes a `multipart/form-data` header that has no `boundary=` — but the XHR path has no such rescue. Upload progress specifics: `onUploadProgress` is an XHR-adapter feature (the browser default; axios's adapter order is `['xhr','http','fetch']`), so it will not report if anything forces the fetch adapter. The progress event gives `loaded`, `total`, `progress`, `rate`, `estimated`, and `total` can be undefined for streamed bodies, so guard it. `onDownloadProgress` is the counterpart for the try-on result.
findings.source: https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/7054 and https://axios.rest/pages/advanced/multipart-form-data-format ("Do not manually set the Content-Type header for browser … FormData"); D:\FYP\frontend\node_modules\axios\dist\node\axios.cjs (`adapter: ['xhr','http','fetch']`, fetch-adapter boundary deletion ~line 5816)

findings.title: AXIOS: the JWT refresh interceptor has three fragile spots — header spreading, the in-flight promise reset, and the hard redirect
findings.detail: In D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\api.ts: (a) on retry it does `original.headers = { ...(original.headers as Record<string,string>), Authorization: … }`, spreading an `AxiosHeaders` class instance into a plain object. It happens to work because AxiosHeaders stores normalised names as own enumerable properties, but it discards the instance's methods and any non-enumerable state — and it's unnecessary, because the request interceptor already attaches `tokens.getAccess()` to every outgoing request, and `tokens.saveAccess()` ran before the retry. (b) `refreshInFlight = refreshInFlight ?? refreshAccessToken()` followed by `refreshInFlight = null` after the await means whichever waiter resumes first nulls the shared promise, so a 401 arriving in that window starts a second refresh; the reset belongs on the promise itself. (c) `window.location.href = "/login"` on refresh failure does a full document reload, throwing away the React tree and the query cache — acceptable as a last resort, but it bypasses the App Router and loses any unsaved form state. Also note the `isAuthCall` guard checks `original?.url`, which for `api` requests is the path relative to baseURL — that works here, but any absolute-URL call would need care.
findings.actionable: Rewrite the retry as: `try { await (refreshInFlight ??= refreshAccessToken().finally(() => { refreshInFlight = null })); return api.request(original) }` — drop the manual header mutation entirely and let the request interceptor re-attach the fresh token. On terminal refresh failure, prefer clearing tokens + `queryClient.clear()` + a router navigation over `window.location.href`, by exposing a logout callback that AppProviders registers with the api module. Keep the `_retried` single-retry marker and the isAuthCall exclusion — both are correct.

findings.title: A11Y: Base UI gives you ARIA, keyboard and focus management — you owe it focus indicators, contrast, and accessible names
findings.detail: Base UI states plainly: it handles ARIA/role attributes, pointer interactions, keyboard navigation and focus management per the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, but "While Base UI components manage focus, it's the developer's responsibility to visually indicate focus" (style `:focus`/`:focus-visible` per the WCAG focus-appearance guidance), to meet colour-contrast minimums (it recommends APCA), and to supply accessible names for custom controls via `alt`/`aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` where no visible label exists. Concretely for this project: the `@layer base { * { @apply … outline-ring/50 } }` plus the components' `focus-visible:ring-3 focus-visible:ring-ring/50` cover most of the focus story — but `--muted-foreground: oklch(0.53 0.02 286)` on `--muted: oklch(0.97 0.004 286)` is the kind of low-contrast pairing that needs checking, and it is used for all placeholder text, select placeholders and dropdown labels.
findings.actionable: Keep `focus-visible:border-ring focus-visible:ring-3 focus-visible:ring-ring/50` on every interactive element you hand-write; never `outline-none` without a replacement ring. Run the light and dark palettes in globals.css through a contrast checker, especially `muted-foreground`-on-`muted` and `muted-foreground`-on-`background` for the 14px placeholder/label text. Test each new feature with keyboard only: Tab to reach it, arrows inside Select/Tabs/Menu, Esc to dismiss, and confirm focus returns to the trigger after a dialog closes.

findings.title: A11Y: dialogs need a Title for their name, icon-only buttons need sr-only text, and `aria-invalid` must be wired from form errors
findings.detail:
Base UI's `Dialog.Title` renders an `

` and is what supplies the dialog's accessible name — a Popup with no Title is announced as an unnamed dialog, and `Dialog.Description` supplies the description. The project's DialogContent already does the icon-button pattern right (`Close`), which is the model for every other icon-only control — the sidebar collapse, the card overflow menus, the delete buttons. Separately, every generated component styles an invalid state (`aria-invalid:border-destructive aria-invalid:ring-3 aria-invalid:ring-destructive/20` on Input, Select trigger, Checkbox, Button) but nothing in the app ever sets `aria-invalid`, so those styles are currently unreachable and error state is invisible to assistive tech. Base UI's `Field.Error` would wire both the styling hook and `aria-describedby` automatically; with plain RHF you must do it yourself.
findings.actionable: Every `<DialogContent>` must contain a `<DialogTitle>` (use `sr-only` on it if the design has no visible heading) and a `<DialogDescription>` when there's explanatory text. Every icon-only button gets a `<span className="sr-only">` label. For each field, render `aria-invalid={!!errors.field}` and `aria-describedby={errors.field ? "field-error" : undefined}` with a matching `id="field-error"` on the message element — or adopt Base UI `Field` and get all of it for free.
