summary: Researched 20+ sources (style guides from Google/Django/Linux kernel, detection research on arXiv/ScienceDirect, HN and arXiv studies of developer complaints about "AI slop", plus verbatim comment samples from Django 5.x, DRF, Sentry, Next.js and TanStack Query) and measured this repo against Django/DRF installed locally. Headline result: comment *density* is NOT the tell (this project runs 6.9% comment lines vs Django's 7.5%, statistically indistinguishable, and the literature openly disagrees on direction). The real tells are shape, voice, and referent: (1) evenly distributed short labels instead of long silences punctuated by rare dense paragraphs (project's median longest uncommented run is 44 lines, Django db/models is 87; project comment blocks average 8.7 words with 5% being 3+ lines, Django 17.8 words with 26% being 3+ lines); (2) teaching voice in second person ("you", "we", "Remember:", "Notice") at 13-15% of comment lines vs 7-8% in Django/DRF, which Django's own style guide explicitly forbids; (3) comments whose referent is the *framework or the reader* rather than *the world outside the code* (no ticket number, no version, no vendor bug, no measured number, nothing falsifiable); (4) ASCII banner rules (87 such lines in 13 files here), which Google's TS guide bans outright; (5) module-top tutorial docstrings, which appear in no production codebase. Positive rules and verbatim exemplars from real Django (hashers.py, DRF views.py), Sentry (Django + TS), Next.js link.tsx and TanStack Query are below, plus grep commands to audit and a list of comments in this repo that are already correct and should be the house style reference.

findings.title: The module-top tutorial docstring is the single strongest tell, and this repo has ~14 of them
findings.detail: Every LLM-written file in this repo opens with a multi-paragraph essay explaining the file's role in the architecture to a newcomer: D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\api.ts lines 1-16 ("The single place where the frontend talks to Django... Two automatic behaviours are set up below: 1. REQUEST interceptor..."), D:\FYP\backend\apps\accounts\serializers.py lines 1-7 ("Serializers = the translator between JSON (what Next.js sends/receives) and Python objects"), D:\FYP\backend\apps\accounts\views.py lines 1-7 ("Views = the actual API endpoints. Each class below becomes one URL. DRF gives us ready-made base classes so we write almost no code:"). No production Django or TS file does this. Django's own modules mostly have no module docstring at all (contrib/auth: 3 of 25 modules, 12%); when they do it is one line. The study of LLM-generated comments in real repositories found detected comments concentrate in the "Explanation" category (52-81% of flagged comments), which is exactly this genre: prose whose job is to teach, not to record.
findings.actionable: Delete or reduce to one line every module docstring in this repo that explains what a layer of Django/React *is*. Specifically: api.ts (16 lines -> 0), tokens.ts (12 -> 0, move the localStorage-vs-cookie trade-off to docs/), use-auth.ts (8 -> 0), types/wardrobe.ts (7 -> 1), accounts/views.py (7 -> 0), accounts/serializers.py (7 -> 0), accounts/models.py (7 -> 1: "Email-based user; Django's default logs in with username."), config/settings.py (keep the no-secrets rule, it is a real project invariant, but cut it to one line).
findings.source: arXiv 2607.01867 An Exploratory Study on LLM-Generated Code and Comments in Code Repositories (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.01867v1); measured locally against D:\FYP\backend\venv\Lib\site-packages\django

findings.title: Second-person / first-person-plural teaching voice: Django's style guide bans it in so many words
findings.detail: Django's contributing style guide states the rule directly: avoid the use of "we" in comments, use the imperative ("Loop over" not "We loop over"). This repo is full of the banned form plus the teacherly imperative aimed at the reader: "(Remember: settings.py made every endpoint login-required by default, so we must opt out here explicitly.)" (accounts/views.py:24), "Notice `email` is read-only" (accounts/serializers.py:20), "Honest trade-off you should know (and can explain if an examiner asks)" (tokens.ts:4), "so you and your teammate never edit the same file" (settings.py:52), "this is what you type to log in" (accounts/models.py:76). I measured it: 13% of comment-ish lines in backend/apps and 15% in frontend/src contain you/your/we/our/remember/notice/obviously/simply, against 7% in django/db/models and 8% in rest_framework. The *kind* of "we" matters too: Sentry's "we are unable to access request.body later on" is a team recording a fact, while "so we never forget it" is a tutor reassuring a student.
findings.actionable: Run `grep -rnE "\b(you|your|Remember|Notice that|obviously|simply|Let's|imagine)\b" --include=*.py --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx backend/apps frontend/src` and rewrite every hit in the imperative or delete it. Hard rule for the project: a comment may never address the reader, and may never address an examiner.

findings.title: Explaining the framework instead of the code (Google's Python guide forbids it verbatim)
findings.detail: Google's Python style guide: "never describe the code. Assume the person reading the code knows Python (though not what you're trying to do) better than you do." This repo repeatedly explains DRF and Django to the reader: "DRF gives us ready-made base classes so we write almost no code: CreateAPIView -> handles POST" (accounts/views.py:4-6), "Tells Django HOW to create users" (accounts/models.py:15), "create_user() hashes the password for us" (accounts/serializers.py:84), "Django's built-in rules: not too short, not all numbers, not a common password" (accounts/serializers.py:77), "lowercases the domain part" next to normalize_email() (accounts/models.py:25). Each of these is a fact about the framework that is one hover or one docs page away, and it will rot when the framework changes. Contrast the same territory in DRF's own source (rest_framework/views.py:143-144): "Exempt all DRF views from Django's LoginRequiredMiddleware. Users should set DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES to 'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated' instead", which records a decision and its consequence, not a lesson.
findings.actionable: Delete every comment that would still be true in a codebase that has nothing to do with this project. Quick test to apply per comment: if it could appear verbatim in the Django tutorial, it does not belong in this repo.

findings.title: ASCII banner comments: banned by name in Google's TypeScript guide, 87 lines of them here
findings.detail: Google's TypeScript style guide: "Comments are not enclosed in boxes drawn with asterisks or other characters." Python style guides likewise discourage banner comments. I counted 87 banner lines across 13 files here: the `// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------` rules in api.ts (lines 37-39, 49-51, 120-122), use-auth.ts (5 pairs), types/wardrobe.ts, vision/storage.py, config/settings.py, and the heavier `# ====...` + centered uppercase heading in wardrobe/views.py:46-48 (`#  CATEGORIES`). Important nuance so you do not over-correct: real production code does use section markers, just undecorated and on one line. DRF's views.py has bare `# Dispatch methods` (line 389), `# API policy instantiation methods` (253), `# API policy implementation methods` (306); generics.py has `# Concrete view classes that provide method handlers / # by composing the mixin classes with the base view.` (185-186). The tell is the ruled line, the symmetry, and the fact that every section gets one whether or not the file is long enough to need navigation.
findings.actionable: Strip all `# ---`/`// ---`/`# ===` rule lines repo-wide (`grep -rlE "(#|//) ?[-=]{4,}" --include=*.py --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx backend frontend/src`). Where a file genuinely needs navigation (wardrobe/views.py is 400+ lines), keep a single bare label line like `# Categories`. Files under ~120 lines get no section markers at all.

findings.title: Docstrings on trivial functions: the real threshold is a written rule, and humans sit far below it
findings.detail: Google's Python guide makes docstrings mandatory only for a function that is (a) part of the public API, (b) of nontrivial size, or (c) has non-obvious logic. A documentation study (COMCAT) measured that human developers in its corpus documented only 18.42% of functions, while the automated tool documented 100%, which is the same signature LLM output has. I measured this repo: 44% of defs+classes in backend/apps carry a docstring, against 21% in django/db/models, 35% in django/contrib/auth, 36% in rest_framework. The worst offenders are the ones that restate the name: `"""What the frontend shows in the navbar."""` on display_name (accounts/models.py:90), `"""Runs after the individual field checks. Good place for cross-field rules."""` on validate() (serializers.py:73), `/** Used after a silent refresh, when only the access token changed. */` on saveAccess (tokens.ts:53), `"""What we get back from processing one photo."""` (vision/background.py:58).
findings.actionable: Delete docstrings on: any function whose body is one to three obvious lines, any DRF validate_*/get_queryset override whose behavior is visible, any @property that returns a formatted field. Keep docstrings on: serializers/views that form the public API contract, anything with a non-obvious invariant (wardrobe/views.py's owner-filtering rule is worth keeping). Target roughly a third of defs, not all of them.
findings.source: https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html ; COMCAT (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.13648); measured locally with an AST scan

findings.title: Density is a trap: the strong signal is DISTRIBUTION (silence punctuated by dense paragraphs)
findings.detail: This is the most useful thing I measured, and it contradicts the usual folklore. Inline comment lines per total lines: this repo's backend 6.9%, django/db/models 7.5%, DRF 5.6%. Indistinguishable. What differs sharply is shape. Median longest run of code with no comment at all: this repo 44 lines, django/db/models 87, django/contrib/auth 56, DRF 52. Average words per comment block: this repo 8.7 (median 5), Django 17.8 (median 13), DRF 12.6. Share of comment blocks that are 3+ lines: this repo 5% (frontend 0%), Django 26%, DRF 15%. So the human pattern is: long stretches of nothing, then a genuinely long comment where something is actually strange. The LLM pattern is a short label sprinkled evenly over everything, roughly one per block of code, none of them long enough to carry real information.
findings.actionable: Two-sided edit, not a deletion pass: (1) delete about two thirds of the one-line labels in backend/apps and frontend/src so that files routinely run 60-90 lines with no comment; (2) promote the three or four comments that carry real information into proper 3-6 line paragraphs. In api.ts the refresh-deduplication logic deserves a real paragraph; the `// 30s` style labels do not deserve to exist.

findings.title: The academic literature contradicts itself on comment volume, which is itself a reason not to use it as a tell
findings.detail: One study of Claude 3 output reports the largest effect sizes distinguishing it from human code were Average Comment Lines, Blank Lines, Comment Lines and Comment-to-Code Ratio, all higher for the model. A large-scale measurement of AI-generated code in real-world repositories reports the opposite direction for merged code. The likely reconciliation: raw model output is comment-heavy, but code that survives review and merge has been trimmed, so "AI-generated code in the wild" looks different from "LLM output". Practical consequence for you: volume-based self-checks ("am I writing too many comments?") are unreliable; voice and referent checks are reliable. Human reviewers, for what it is worth, score about 50% (chance) at spotting LLM code snippet-by-snippet, which is why the tells that do work are file-level and stylistic rather than line-level.
findings.actionable: Do not set a comment-ratio target in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md. Set rules about voice, referent and placement instead (see the checklist items in this list). They are the ones that survive contact with evidence.

findings.title: Unfalsifiable comments vs comments that make a checkable claim about the outside world
findings.detail: This is the deepest tell I found, and it is the one to internalize: real comments point at something outside the file that could be checked or could change, and LLM comments point at the code itself. Real Django: "# Database-level options are not supported, see #21961." (db/models/fields/__init__.py:158), "# could be affected by `manager.clear()`. Refs #19816." (related_descriptors.py:955), "# Ancient versions of Django created plain MD5 passwords and accepted MD5 passwords with an empty salt." (contrib/auth/hashers.py:175-176), "# Run the default password hasher once to reduce the timing difference between an existing user with an unusable password and a nonexistent user or missing hasher (similar to #20760)." (hashers.py:52-54), "# RemovedInDjango60Warning." (db/models/base.py). Real TanStack Query: "The timeout is sometimes triggered 1 ms before the stale time expiration. To mitigate this issue we always add 1 ms to the timeout." Real Next.js: "// in dev, we only prefetch on hover to avoid wasting resources as the prefetch will trigger compiling the page." Each of these asserts a fact that could be false. The LLM comment ("so we never forget it", "the user sees nothing", "that is the whole point of having them") cannot be false, because it describes intent rather than reality.
findings.actionable: Adopa a single acceptance test before writing any comment in this repo: name the thing outside this function that makes the comment true (a ticket, an HTTP status, a browser/SDK bug, a Cloudinary quirk, a measured timing, a Django version). If you cannot name one, either the comment is restating the code (delete it) or it belongs in docs/ (move it).

findings.title: Annotating every element of a list: the exhaustive-enumeration tell, live in settings.py
findings.detail: D:\FYP\backend\config\settings.py annotates every single entry of THIRD_PARTY_APPS and LOCAL_APPS ("# the API toolkit", "# login tokens", "# lets localhost:3000 call localhost:8000", "# users, login, profile", "# saved outfits, wear log", ...). A human annotates the one entry that would surprise a reader ("django.contrib.postgres  # ArrayField, full-text search helpers" earns its keep; "rest_framework  # the API toolkit" does not). Same pattern in accounts/models.py where each field group gets a `# ---- Identity ----` label and USERNAME_FIELD/REQUIRED_FIELDS each get an aligned trailing comment. The LLM instinct is to complete the pattern across all members of a set; the human instinct is to flag the exception. The same instinct shows up in the detection literature as "ChatGPT-generated code adheres more closely to coding standards", i.e. suspiciously uniform.
findings.actionable: In settings.py keep trailing comments only on entries a reader would otherwise have to look up (django.contrib.postgres, django_filters, drf_spectacular); delete the rest. In accounts/models.py drop the `# ---- X ----` field-group labels and the aligned trailing comments; keep help_text (that is user-facing and earns its place).
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2306.14397 (Discriminating Human-authored from ChatGPT-Generated Code Via Discernable Feature Analysis)

findings.title: Defensive wrappers plus an explanatory header: the try/except tell, and the duplication data behind it
findings.detail: D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\tokens.ts is the textbook case: a header paragraph explaining why everything is wrapped ("Everything is wrapped in try/catch because localStorage throws in some browsers..."), then three near-identical functions safeGet/safeSet/safeRemove, each repeating the `typeof window === "undefined"` guard and each carrying its own apologetic comment (`/* storage blocked - ignore */`, `/* ignore */`). Developer complaints catalogued in the "AI slop" literature name exactly this pattern (redundant repeated guards, "checks if (array && array.length > 0) five times in a row"), and GitClear's measurement of 211M changed lines gives it a number: duplicated code blocks rose ~8x in 2024, and for the first time copy/paste exceeded moved (refactored) code, with moved lines falling from 24.8% of changes in 2021 to 9.5% in 2024. The comment is not the real problem; it is advertising the duplication.
findings.actionable: Collapse tokens.ts to one guarded accessor (e.g. `function storage(): Storage | null` returning null on the server or when access throws) used by all three operations, then the explanation shrinks to one line at that one function and the three apologetic comments disappear. This is the general move: when you find yourself writing the same comment three times, the comment is telling you to extract a function.
findings.source: https://www.gitclear.com/ai_assistant_code_quality_2025_research ; https://arxiv.org/html/2603.27249v3 ("An Endless Stream of AI Slop")

findings.title: Typographic punctuation: already clean here, but keep the guard, and know the real code-specific variants
findings.detail: I grepped all of frontend/src, backend/apps and backend/config for non-ASCII and found zero hits, so the em-dash/smart-quote tell does not currently apply to this repo. Worth knowing anyway: the em dash became the popular AI tell through 2025 (it is U+2014, greppable), though the claim is contested since em dashes have always been human; what actually reads as generated is the *cluster*: em dashes plus curly quotes plus arrows plus checkmark/emoji in comments. The code-specific variants that DO show up here are ASCII cousins of the same instinct: aligned ASCII arrow tables in docstrings ("CreateAPIView        -> handles POST", "GET   /api/auth/me/   -> who am I"), and trailing comments column-aligned across consecutive lines (accounts/models.py:25-27, 76-77). Hand-written code rarely maintains that alignment because maintaining it costs work on every edit.
findings.actionable: Add a CI/pre-commit grep: `grep -rnP "[^\x00-\x7F]" --include=*.py --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx backend/apps backend/config frontend/src` must stay empty (except where a literal genuinely needs it). Separately, remove the arrow tables in accounts/views.py:5-6 and 63-64 and stop column-aligning trailing comments.

findings.title: Prose-level LLM tells that leak into comments: the named-label opener, the balanced pair, the triad
findings.detail: The HN "Various LLM Smells" thread is the best concrete catalogue I found of the prose patterns, and they do leak into comments and commit messages: the "The [label]:" opener ("The honest caveat:", "The smoking gun:", "The thing to internalize:"); clustered intensity words (real/genuine/actual, "what really happens"); three-clause lists where the third clause combines the first two; figurative jargon used indiscriminately ("load bearing", "blast radius", "escape hatch", "belt-and-suspenders", "smoke test" where "sanity check" fits); and the two-sentence comment whose second sentence restates the first as a contrast ("not just X, but Y"). In this repo the same instinct appears as the rhetorical question header ("Why React Query instead of plain useState + useEffect?" in use-auth.ts:6) followed by a balanced three-bullet answer, and the reassurance clause ("The user sees nothing.", api.ts:15).
findings.actionable: Ban three constructions in this repo's comments and commit messages: the rhetorical question header, the bulleted list inside a comment, and the reassurance/summary clause at the end of a comment. If a comment has bullets, it is documentation: move it to docs/ or the README.

findings.title: Uniformity is a tell, but do not fake sloppiness; remove the artificial polish instead
findings.detail: The feature-analysis work on distinguishing ChatGPT code identified 22 layout/structural features (comment ratio, blank-line ratio, indentation length, average nesting depth, average parameter count) and reached 90%+ classification accuracy, concluding that "ChatGPT-generated code adheres more closely to coding standards compared to human-authored code" and that "human code frequently exhibits remnants of development iterations, such as commented-out code snippets, which are absent in ChatGPT-generated code". It also notes humans use abbreviations and ambiguous short identifiers while models pick uniformly meaningful words. The actionable reading is not "write worse code": it is that the *comments and docstrings* in an LLM file all share one template (same length, same opening verb, same 2-paragraph shape), and a human file's comments are wildly uneven in length and register because each was written at a different moment for a different reason.
findings.actionable: When you finish a file, read only its comments in sequence. If they look like a set (same length, same shape, one per block), rewrite: keep the two that matter and make them different lengths from each other. Do not add commented-out code or deliberate typos to seem human; that is cargo-culting the symptom.

findings.title: What real comments actually contain, with measured proportions (the taxonomy to aim at)
findings.detail: Pascarella and Bacchelli manually classified 40,000+ comment lines across 14 Java OSS projects into 6 top-level and 16 fine-grained categories, then counted them. From the paper's figure (blocks / lines): Summary 5,346/7,344; Expand 199/1,995; Rationale 256/563; Purpose total 5,801/8,165. Usage 2,904/3,332; Exception 244/336; Deprecation 54/63; Notice total 3,202/3,731. TODO 190/248; Incomplete 87/111; Commented-out code 329/684; Under-development total 606/1,043. Directive 1,023/1,241; Formatter 57/73. License 1,023/11,369; Ownership 564/1,021; Pointer (links/references) 1,729/1,972. Two lessons. First, pure Rationale is rare (563 lines out of ~29k): the "always explain why" slogan oversells how often a why-comment is warranted, which is why an LLM file that explains why at every step reads wrong. Second, Pointer comments (links and cross-references) are more than 3x as common as Rationale: the most characteristic human inline comment is a pointer to something elsewhere, not an explanation.
findings.actionable: Give each comment you write a category before you write it: Rationale, Notice/Usage (caller-facing constraint), Pointer (ticket/docs/vendor bug), or TODO. If it is a Summary, it belongs in a docstring on a public interface, not inline. If it fits no category, delete it.
findings.source: Pascarella & Bacchelli, "Classifying code comments in Java open-source software systems", MSR 2017 (https://sback.it/publications/msr2017a.pdf), figures extracted from the PDF

findings.title: Positive rules for Django, with verbatim exemplars from the Django and DRF you have installed
findings.detail: Verified in D:\FYP\backend\venv\Lib\site-packages. (1) Ticket pointers for the weird line: "# Refs #12057." (db/models/base.py:534), "# Database-level options are not supported, see #21961." (fields/__init__.py:158), "# the corresponding None parameter. See ticket #10888." (sql/compiler.py:1709). (2) Historical/compat facts: "# Ancient versions of Django created plain MD5 passwords..." (hashers.py:175). (3) Security reasoning where it is genuinely subtle, 3-4 lines, no preamble: hashers.py:52-54 and 62-65. (4) Deprecation markers as bare tags: "# RemovedInDjango60Warning." (5) Class-attribute contracts as `#` comments above the attributes rather than docstrings: DRF generics.py:28-38 ("# You'll need to either set these attributes, or override `get_queryset()`/`get_serializer_class()`. If you are overriding a view method, it is important that you call `get_queryset()` instead of accessing the `queryset` property directly, as `queryset` will get evaluated only once..."). (6) Blunt self-criticism: "# XXX: The UX does not support multiple selected values." (contrib/admin/widgets.py:273), "# FIXME: Allow to override this." (core/handlers/asgi.py:155), "# HACK: datetime instances cannot be assigned new attributes. Define a subclass" (templatetags/tz.py:12). Tone throughout: imperative or declarative third person, lowercase after the marker, one clause unless the subtlety genuinely needs four lines, never a greeting, never a recap.
findings.actionable: Use these as the house style. Concretely for this repo: replace accounts/views.py's RegisterView docstring with nothing and keep only a one-line note if a non-obvious decision exists; keep wardrobe/views.py's owner-filtering invariant but as a 2-line comment on get_queryset rather than a module essay; write `# Cloudinary rejects > 10 MB on the free plan` style pointers instead of "Phone photos are big, but 12 MB is already generous".

findings.title: Sentry is the closest real-world analogue to this project (production Django + TypeScript) and its comments are the model
findings.detail: From getsentry/sentry src/sentry/api/base.py, verbatim: "# I don't know why, but unless we declare these loggers earlier, we run into circular import errors." (admitting ignorance while recording an empirical fact, which no LLM writes); "# XXX: without this seemingly useless access to `.body` we are unable to access `request.body` later on due to `rest_framework` loading the request body via `request.read()`" (names the exact mechanism and the exact library); "# XXX: Since DRF 3.x, when the request is passed into `initialize_request` it's set as an internal variable on the returned request. Then when we call `rv.auth` it attempts to authenticate, fails and sets `user` and `auth` to None on the internal request. We keep track of these here and reassign them as needed." (a long comment, earned, version-scoped); "# TODO(jstanley): Temporary logging to explain agent-token 401s... Remove once the auth issue is resolved." (named owner + exit condition); and short situational ones: "# Only enforced in dev environment", "# Only convert args when using defined handlers". Note what is absent: no module tutorial, no banners, no docstring on every method, and the docstrings that exist are 1-3 lines of contract ("If response is paginated, it will have a 'Link' header").
findings.actionable: Two habits to copy immediately: (1) when you do not know why something is needed, say so and say what happens without it, rather than inventing a rationale; (2) every TODO gets an owner and a removal condition. Sweep the repo for bare TODOs and give them both.

findings.title: Positive rules for TypeScript, with verbatim exemplars from Next.js, TanStack Query and Sentry's frontend
findings.detail: Next.js packages/next/src/client/link.tsx: "// adding this to the publicly exported type currently breaks existing apps", "// WARNING: This should be an interface to prevent TypeScript from inlining it in declarations of libraries depending on Next.js. Not trivial to reproduce so only convert to an interface when needed.", "// If we've already fetched the key, then don't prefetch it again!", "// in dev, we only prefetch on hover to avoid wasting resources as the prefetch will trigger compiling the page.", "// TODO-APP: Include the full set of Anchor props", "// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars". TanStack query-core: "This property keeps track of the last query with defined data. It will be used to pass the previous data and query to the placeholder function between renders.", "The timeout is sometimes triggered 1 ms before the stale time expiration. To mitigate this issue we always add 1 ms to the timeout.", "a stored select error belongs to previously selected data; once that data is gone (query switch or reset), it must not leak into this result". Sentry static/app/utils/queryClient.tsx: "// Overrides to the default react-query options.", "// See https://tanstack.com/query/v5/docs/framework/react/guides/important-defaults", "// Disable retries for client errors that won't succeed on retry". Pattern: sentence fragments, lowercase start, frequently no terminal period, one line unless the mechanism truly needs five, `/** */` reserved for exported API, and a link when the reason lives in someone else's docs.
findings.actionable: Rewrite the comments in api.ts and use-auth.ts in this register. E.g. api.ts's refresh block becomes one earned paragraph above `refreshInFlight` explaining the stampede and the single-promise fix, plus `// plain axios: using `api` here would re-enter this interceptor` above the axios.post. Delete the `// treat as fresh for 5 minutes` / `// 30s` labels (the code says that). Keep `// Do not even try if there is no token - avoids a pointless 401 on first load`, which is a real decision.

findings.title: The four style-guide rules worth pinning in AGENTS.md, quoted
findings.detail: Google TypeScript guide: "Use /** JSDoc */ comments for documentation, i.e. comments a user of the code should read. Use // line comments for implementation comments, i.e. comments that only concern the implementation of the code itself"; multi-line implementation comments "must use multiple single-line comments (//-style), not block comment style"; "Comments are not enclosed in boxes drawn with asterisks or other characters"; omit documentation that is redundant with the types (do not write `/** @param x A number. */ function foo(x: number)`); document all top-level exports. Google Python guide: docstring required only for public API / nontrivial size / non-obvious logic; "never describe the code"; "The final place to have comments is in tricky parts of the code. If you're going to have to explain it at the next code review, you should comment it now"; TODO format is `# TODO: <link to bug> - <action>`. Linux kernel: "Comments are good, but there is also a danger of over-commenting. NEVER try to explain HOW your code works in a comment: it's much better to write the code so that the working is obvious, and it's a waste of time to explain badly written code" and "try to avoid putting comments inside a function body: if the function is so complex that you need to separately comment parts of it, you should probably go back to chapter 6". Django: avoid "we"; wrap comments and docstrings at 79 columns; test docstrings state the behavior without "Tests that..."; reserve ticket references for obscure issues, with the number at the end of a sentence.
findings.actionable: Add a short COMMENTS section to D:\FYP\frontend\AGENTS.md and the backend equivalent with exactly these rules plus the falsifiability test from the unfalsifiable-comments finding. Keep it under 12 lines so it is actually followed.

findings.title: A 9-rule review checklist that maps cleanly onto the tells
findings.detail: The Stack Overflow blog's widely cited rules, verbatim: (1) Comments should not duplicate the code. (2) Good comments do not excuse unclear code. (3) If you can't write a clear comment, there may be a problem with the code. (4) Comments should dispel confusion, not cause it. (5) Explain unidiomatic code in comments. (6) Provide links to the original source of copied code. (7) Include links to external references where they will be most helpful. (8) Add comments when fixing bugs. (9) Use comments to mark incomplete implementations. Rules 5-9 are precisely the categories LLM comments under-produce (unidiomatic code, provenance of copied code, external links, bug-fix context, incompleteness) while rule 1 names what they over-produce. That asymmetry is a better detector than any single surface feature.
findings.actionable: Use rules 5-9 as a positive prompt when commenting this repo: the places that deserve comments are the unidiomatic bits (the DRF TokenObtainPairSerializer subclass, the Cloudinary folder conventions, the EXIF rotation handling, the refresh-token stampede guard), anything copied from a blog or SO answer (link it), and anything left half-done (mark it with owner + condition).

findings.title: Comments already correct in this repo: use them as the in-house reference, do not strip them
findings.detail: Not everything here reads generated, and the good ones are a useful calibration set. D:\FYP\backend\apps\vision\background.py:92-93: "# EXIF rotation: phone photos often carry \"rotate 90 degrees\" as metadata rather than in the pixels. Without this, shirts come out sideways." (checkable fact about the outside world, plus the concrete failure mode). background.py:33-34: "# The model is loaded once and kept in memory. Loading it per request would add several seconds to every upload." (decision plus cost of the alternative). D:\FYP\backend\apps\wardrobe\views.py:63: "# Only so the docs generator can see the model; get_queryset() is what runs." (explains a line that would otherwise look like a bug). D:\FYP\frontend\src\lib\api.ts:63-64: "// Plain axios, not `api` - otherwise this call would be intercepted too and we would loop forever." (names the failure mode). D:\FYP\frontend\src\hooks\use-auth.ts:41: "retry: false, // a failed /me/ means \"not logged in\", retrying will not help".
findings.actionable: Quote these five in AGENTS.md as "this is what a comment in this repo looks like". Every comment being added should be defensible by analogy to one of them; anything that cannot be is a deletion candidate.

findings.title: Tells that live in the code rather than the comments (reviewers weight these heavily)
findings.detail: From the arXiv study of 1,154 Reddit/HN posts on AI-assisted development and related reviewer accounts: oversized PRs ("it's like 1-2k lines of code and after looking at it for 5 minutes I can tell it's pretty much entirely AI generated"); emoji in comments ("if the comment has an emoji it's a guarantee"); `setTimeout` as a band-aid; casting to `any` to silence type errors; tests edited to pass instead of code fixed; mocks for services that do not exist; duplicated logic rather than reuse; and the decisive one in practice, the author being unable to explain their own code when asked. GitClear quantifies the duplication side (8x rise in duplicated blocks; refactored/"moved" lines down from 24.8% to 9.5% of changes). CodeRabbit now ships automated "slop detection" on PRs (aimed at empty functions, fake documentation, inflated comments) though it does not publish its heuristics, and it exempts known collaborators to limit false positives.
findings.actionable: For this project: keep commits small and topical; never use `any` or `@ts-ignore` without a one-line reason comment naming what is being suppressed; never add a `setTimeout` without a comment stating what race it papers over and what the real fix would be; and before committing a file, be able to explain each line out loud (the explanation belongs in your head or the PR body, not as a comment on every line).

findings.title: Concrete audit commands for this repo (run these as the de-LLM pass)
findings.detail: Four greps cover most of the measurable tells, and all four were used to produce the numbers in this report. Banner rules: `grep -rnE "(#|//) ?[-=]{4,}" --include=*.py --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx backend frontend/src` (currently 87 hits in 13 files). Reader-address and teaching voice: `grep -rnE "\b(you|your|we|our|Remember|Notice|obviously|simply|Let's)\b" --include=*.py --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx backend/apps backend/config frontend/src` (currently ~13-15% of comment lines, target under 8% and zero second person). Non-ASCII: `grep -rnP "[^\x00-\x7F]"` over the same paths (currently zero, keep it there). Trivial docstrings: a 20-line AST script that flags any FunctionDef with a docstring and a body of three statements or fewer (currently 44% of defs carry docstrings vs Django's 21-35%).
findings.actionable: Put the first three greps in a pre-commit hook or a `make lint-comments` target. They are cheap, they produce zero false positives for banners and non-ASCII, and they would have caught every instance flagged in this report.

findings.title: The one-paragraph version of the style to adopt
findings.detail: Write code that needs few comments, then comment only four things: a constraint the caller must know (put it in a docstring on the public interface, one to three lines, no preamble); a decision whose alternative a future reader would otherwise try (one clause, naming the alternative and why it loses); a pointer to the thing that explains the weirdness (ticket, issue URL, vendor doc, version); and unfinished work (TODO plus owner plus removal condition). Never explain the language, the framework, or the reader's own next line. Never address the reader. Never draw a box. Let files run 60-90 lines in silence, then spend five real lines where something is genuinely strange. Prefer a comment that could be proven wrong over one that merely sounds wise.
findings.actionable: Paste this paragraph into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md as the comment policy, then do one pass over the 13 files listed in the banner grep and the 14 files with module docstrings. That single pass removes the large majority of what makes this codebase read as machine-written.
